title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
body_text: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii | Virtually Fun --> --> --> --> --> Skip to primary content Virtually Fun Fun with Virtualization Search Main menu Home Privacy Policy Qemu Post navigation ← Previous My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii Posted on October 29, 2026 by Rairii (This is a guest post by Rairii) Mac OS 7.6 booting on the Wii Mac OS 9.2.2 booted on the Wii So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far. But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s? Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything. Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead. I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies). I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot. So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually. The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel. Additionally, the Trampoline expects that physical addresses from 0x8000_0000 onwards corresponds to memory mapped I/O (on existing systems this code ran on, this would correspond to PCI-bus address space). This is not the case here, and in fact on Wii U, this address would correspond to part of RAM. There was also another assumption that broke on these systems, with holes between areas of RAM in the physical address space, some of which were partially filled by memory-mapped I/O. The way I fixed this was to patch the initialisation of this MMIO mapping in the kernel memory chunk list, to a map of physical address 0x0100_0000 (partway through one area of RAM) to virtual address 0xE000_0000 , with length 0x1000_0000 . This specifically maps the whole of the MMIO, plus the end of one RAM area and (for post-GameCube systems) the start of another. (I may change this in future, as on the Wii U, physical address range 0xD000_0000-0xEFFF_FFFF is mapped to a part of the Radeon R7xx GPU called “HDP”, which can be used to map a view of physical memory with specific swizzling and/or endianness swapping, such that a texture in some GPU-specific format can appear to be a linear framebuffer. It depends on whether I need to use this block ) The function used for initialising a mapping in the Trampoline changed at some point and I ended up detecting the older version and hooking the function so I could work around it (earlier versions used a 16-bit page count, later versions used 32-bit). Additionally, older versions of the Trampoline sets up unconditional 1:1 mappings for physical memory above 0x8000_0000 , which needs to be removed as they conflict with the mappings set up earlier. There follows various assorted patches that assume specific hardware. These include: patching out setting some bitflags which correspond to the presence of a microcontroller found on all PowerPC Macintosh hardware, attempting to recalculate the bus frequency using a specific hardware timer, and various register writes and fixups related to a specific interrupt controller device (it’s little endian because it’s on the PCI bus, and naturally, not present here). Finally, the final call to jump into the loaded kernel initialisation code is hooked so additional patches can be made later after everything is loaded into memory. Additionally, the device tree must be hacked up a bit to be in a shape the Trampoline will accept. The interrupt controller is faked to be one of the recognised ones (the little endian one from above, because at a register level it’s closest to the Flipper interrupt controller present on all the ArtX chipsets, albeit on Wii U it was changed somewhat to add support for the additional PowerPC cores). The address of the frame buffer in the device tree is changed to the uncached virtual address (in the 0xExxx_xxxx mapping), and finally a fake Mac99-compatible power management device is added to the device tree, so the Trampoline prepares a power management driver for it, that can be replaced later. As mentioned above, the kernel initialisation is hooked so extra patches can be made. On the kernel side, there is only one patch to be made: the kernel contains several interrupt controller drivers, the one chosen is patched to match the Flipper interrupt controller, with one of the unused ones sacrificed to gain more space for this. The main difference here is that the expected interrupt controller (whose driver is patched) has a legacy mode where it raises a PowerPC interrupt whenever the interrupts change (not just when interrupts are raised) so this needs to be worked around by masking the raised interrupts in the kernel and then unmasking them later on in drivers’ interrupt handlers. Additional patches are made in the “SuperMario” m68k code, and in PowerPC native executables. The m68k code has various codepaths that read and write directly to native interrupt controller registers, these need to be patched. The function pointers for enabling and disabling audio interrupts need to be stubbed out (there’s already an entry in that table that points to a stub, which is helpful). A function called early in the boot process to initialise the ADB and power management microcontroller does not check if the hardware actually exists, and if it doesn’t it clobbers parts of low memory. A function for initialising hardware interrupts has a bug due to a copy-paste blunder, the intent was to skip past the code for initialising the interrupt for serial port 2 if the hardware isn’t present, but the developers forgot to change the jump label when copy-pasting the code from serial port 1, which causes an infinite loop if serial port 2 doesn’t exist. As for native code, there’s more code that reads and writes to interrupt controller registers which needs to be correctly patched. The USBShimKeyboard driver initialisation code fails to handle the state where no USB controller exists and in that case will call a NULL pointer inside the m68k emulator. The power management driver mentioned above is also replaced entirely here (currently I use the stub driver from BlueBox but plan to write my own later to add proper support for shutting down and restarting). All of this is enough to get the TBXI to boot to blinking floppy – after that I wrote a display driver (thanks to Elliott Nunn for his virtio driver, it was very helpful) so I could see it correctly, followed by a driver for the gamecube controller ports (porting from my NT driver for the same) so I could move the mouse cursor around without USB. At this point I started to implement a block IO driver (for EXI devices), but ended up getting stuck thinking about how to deal with how the disk format should be laid out and how the driver should work. Then Mac OS for CHRP got dumped, and I got sidetracked with patching up the later TBXI images to boot it , thinking running 7.x would be useful on a GameCube which doesn’t even have enough RAM to support 8.0 at minimum requirements, and after that I got sidetracked with other projects. Almost a year later I came back to it, implemented my preferred disk format in OpenBIOS and decided to hack up a driver faking SCSI (some other drivers did this, most notably classic Mac OS drivers for various SATA controllers). There were a few issues I found when writing the fake-SCSI driver too: I had to add another patch to the m68k code to force loading the disk driver (and I mean this, a driver loaded from the disk itself, basically implementing the actual disk devices on top of some partitioned block device) as a newer type rather than the older type (the older type was effectively obsolete when the first PowerPC systems released anyway, and I don’t even support the old-style calls from my fake SCSI driver, which is probably why it crashed trying to load it as an older type driver), and also found an interesting quirk where the optical disc driver (loaded from the block device itself) emulates 512-byte sectors on 2048- or 2352-byte sector block devices by making a read call setting up 3 scatter-gather buffers, except it never checked if the underlying SCSI driver actually supports scatter-gather, so I had to implement support for that on reads. I still saw a blinking floppy though, some debugging showed me what was being rejected, a PowerPC function StartLib!GetStartupDevice was being called to get the boot device, and it made some assumptions of both the device tree and that there was some kind of built in SCSI device that needed separate handling. The first one was simple enough (fix the device tree in my driver’s initialisation code), the second one was more interesting in that I had to grovel into internal structures to fix an index in 3 different places (including the device tree) to ensure it was non-zero and so the correct code path would be executed. With this done I saw a happy Mac icon for the first time, but then got rejected by the HFS boot sector (something errored and it returned). This turned out to be a bug in my own driver: I was debugging in dolphin with a hacked up EXI-IDE device; reading and writing data in PIO mode for IDE devices deals in 16-bit words, and I didn’t expect my code to get passed a completely unaligned odd buffer address (low 4 bits equal to 1), so I had to modify my low level driver to not even attempt EXI DMA for such an address. The bug manifested as a byte effectively failing to be written out, with remaining data getting offset by one byte; at least this happened when reading the header of a resource fork, and what failed was the validity checks for this data, making it much easier to debug (I ended up dumping RAM and comparing with the expected data from the disk image I was using). After this, Mac OS 9.2.2 started to boot in my hacked up Dolphin tree, very slowly. It took an hour before it finally crashed, and then I tried 7.6, which also crashed, but earlier. I realised that it was probably crashing trying to load MacsBug, removed it, and after about 20 minutes I was staring at the desktop. Mac OS 7.6 booted in my hacked up Dolphin tree The following morning I tested on real hardware (using SD over SPI). This basically booted 7.6 within 40 seconds, and this was supposed to be the slowest access mode for an SD card! My previous experience was writing an NT driver for SD over SPI though, and perhaps that is more of an outlier. See this video installing NT on a GameCube using such a block device, and note that the NT text setup file copy is sped up 64 times – it’s VERY slow. The difference here is that I get to hog the whole CPU when performing a transfer – in fact there’s no other option, if I return a value specifying the transfer is asynchronous, the caller proceeds to busy-wait for interrupts in a loop waiting for the transfer to complete (although the busy-wait does check for all controllers present on the system). Later on I added some hacked up crash handler so I could try to debug what was going on with MacsBug… it turned out to be an emulation error, no such crash occured when loading MacsBug on real hardware. I then found out the reason Mac OS 9.2.2 was crashing on boot was because of Open Transport, removing it from the Extensions folder caused it to boot perfectly fine. My guess is that Open Transport can’t handle no serial or network device being present at all. As I mentioned, my port is still nowhere near release. Next up will be bringing up the Wii’s SD controller, then the USB controller (I’ve already done some reversing work related to that, I know there’s a vibecoded EHCI driver now, that’ll probably only aid in reversing work really), then getting the port brought up on the Wii U. At some point I want to play around with patches for blowing through at least some of the RAM barriers too. This entry was posted in Macintosh , MacOS , powerpc , Uncategorized by Rairii . title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
body_text: Agents in Games · Labs Home Projects QM Contact Agents in Games Minecraft Civ50 Bed Wars Mindustry The setup What we saw Funny bloopers Run your own swarm Open questions Agents in Games October 2026 Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. Minecraft Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon . We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness Civ50 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. plans/settlement.md Download Settlement coordination (Ada) Primary storage Greta: (1526,70,1507), crafting table (1526,70,1505). Other storage Mabel: double chest (1510,71,1516); Cleo: (1526,71,1523). Cleo building hub shelter; Bram stone mining. Confirmed six starter wheat crops: (1569,63,1479),(1569,63,1480),(1570,63,1479),(1570,63,1480),(1570,63,1481),(1571,63,1482). Preserve farmland, expand riverside farming. Do not harvest immature wheat. Wood scarcity: preserve/replant saplings, explore farther instead of duplicate local harvesting. Nursery around spawn and south-west. Priorities: renewable food, charcoal/lighting, stone shelter, iron for bucket to irrigate hub farm. Avoid redundant new storage. Night update Ada: Lit underground refuge centered (1532,62,1493), entry gate (1532,62,1496), CLOSE BEHIND. Cobble flanks secured x1531/1533 y62–63 z1496. Surface staircase starts (1532,69,1500); Cleo repairing. Food kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493); table (1528,62,1493). Tamsin coordinates food priorities and dawn hunting (Hugo+Rafe). Basil health9.5 food6 urgent; Esme health8 food16; Tamsin health9 food15. Silas holds hoe, Zane plants riverside at dawn. Logs: Tove delivered29 oak to chest (1511,71,1516). Forest east (1700,68,1508), NW grove (1380–1420,z1380). Preserve saplings and livestock breeding pairs. Avoid night surface: witch near (1527,71,1512). Ada’s settlement plan, from the archived shared machine. Following Vera during the first night, 8:09–12:05 into the run, at 2x speed. The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned. Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him. While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider. 22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks. Activity data from the original report. Night shading is approximate. The first-night count in the text is the 22 deaths before minute 20. Two of them fall outside the shaded band. Download the data . After the third night, Ada wrote: “Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.” plans/food-operations.md Download FOOD OPERATIONS — Ada Current constraint: hungry workforce; stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks. 1. Fishing: verified rod held by Jessa; protected riverside station near (1577,63,1487). Report catches and cook before distributing. Use named reserved chest withdrawals, never crowded tosses. 2. Ration tracking: Ines maintains /shared/notes/food-queue.md. Confirm actual recipient inventory and eating before marking served. Tool pickup attribution alone is insufficient. 3. Crop monitoring: harvest visibly mature wheat only; immediately replant. Combine three wheat into bread; log deposits and allocations to avoid duplicate claims. 4. Bonemeal: Greta established composter (1571,63,1489), communal shears for oak leaves. Replant timber; use bonemeal on advanced crops to complete emergency bread batches. 5. Expansion: follow Noor's /shared/plans/food-expansion.md in stages using surplus seeds after mandatory replanting. Buckets already exist; avoid duplicate crafting. Use fed growers, not hunger-critical residents. 6. Logistics: kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493), refuge double chest (1534–1535,62,1492); gate (1532,62,1496), close behind. By dawn it was a "civic priority" and the main cellar. Refuge replay, above . Bed Wars We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills. Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map. A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won. In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count. Takeaways The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game. The setup Mindustry is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this! It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core. This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world. We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment. Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team. Multi-agent swarms, like in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident , can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future. What we saw #1 GPTs act more like a hive GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning). #2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack. Each dot is an agent, sized by the messages it sent; lines show each agent’s strongest ties. Leaders are named. #3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by. Game 7, at about 38:40: the Claude team chat (top) and the GPT team chat (bottom), scrolling in the replay. GPT messages like “G7T5FIRSTcourierLIVE” run words together. The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback. Left, spaces as a share of each team’s chat characters in each game; right, the 28 Claudes who answered one focus-fire proposal with +1 in game 6, plotted by minute. #4 Roles harden, leaders stay put As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes. Filled dots mark who led the army or fleet in each game, hollow dots who proposed rules, and the dot under each game is its winner, grey for Claude and off-white for GPT. #5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web. How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!) Multi-Agent Mindustry : the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run. Multi-Agent Harbor : the framework that runs them, our fork of Harbor , the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it. Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves. We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves. Open Questions Combining model families How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off) Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows? How different initial prompts affect the swarm Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team? Building something? Apply to YC .

title: Breaking the open web won't stop the bad bots
body_text: Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots | TechPolicy.Press Home Topics Newsletter Podcast Series Contributors About Donate Perspective Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots Lila Bailey, Tess Vartanian / Oct 27, 2026 A close up of a spider in its web. Valeriia Neganova/ Unsplash Republish Share Late last month , more than 300 representatives from major media outlets were on Capitol Hill to advocate for the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act . They came with a legitimate grievance. Newsrooms are being hit by a surge of automated traffic, mostly from AI developers. AI developers extract enormous volumes of online content and then potentially deprive website owners of referral traffic and ad revenue with generative AI features and chatbots trained on that content. It is a real problem that deserves a real solution. But this bill doesn’t directly target the harms caused by abusive crawling. Instead, it would force anyone accessing a website automatically to identify themselves and their purposes for collecting public information. Rather than protect journalists, the bill threatens a basic tool they, and many others, rely on to gather information online. Cutting-edge investigative journalism relies on automated data collection. In 2022, a Pulitzer-winning Wall Street Journal investigation analyzed over 31,000 financial disclosures from 12,000 senior government employees, revealing that nearly a quarter of federal officials traded stock in industries their agencies regulated. To conduct an investigation at that scale, the Journal relied on web scraping: an automated process where a software bot, known as a crawler, browses the internet and collects information. This fundamental tool of the open web is now under threat from bills that purport to target “stealth crawling,” but in reality would hamper legitimate public-interest activities, including preservation, journalism, research, and security. Again, aggressive, large-scale scraping is a real problem — particularly as demand for AI training and content has exploded. It can overwhelm websites, increase costs, and threaten institutions that produce and preserve knowledge, including commercial publishers, Wikipedia , libraries , and the Internet Archive , where one of the authors of this piece works. In an apparent attempt to reduce or eliminate problematic scraping practices, proposed bills, like the federal Stealth Bot Prohibition Act and New York’s Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, would impose sweeping prohibitions on anonymous scraping without addressing the real harms. Both bills define a “bot” or “crawler” as software that “retrieves, scans, indexes, scrapes, or otherwise accesses a website or other internet source.” A bot is “stealth” if it fails to disclose its identity and the “specific nature and purpose of the bot.” Under the federal bill, the FTC can pursue penalties of up to $53,000 if a person uses a stealth bot in a way that is “reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden” a website’s “technical or commercial operation.” The bill provides no definition or standard of what is reasonably likely to impair a website. Under the New York bill, which only applies to covered news sites, a publisher can obtain a subpoena to unmask a crawler’s identity without requiring a showing of any harm. Knowing the identity behind a crawler tells us relatively little about whether its behavior is harmful. Under the New York bill, a company that discloses its identity and then accesses the website 10,000 times a minute complies with the law even though it is still imposing enormous and likely unjustified costs on the site. But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not. Many of the most socially valuable uses of crawling require anonymity. Revealing a crawler’s identity and purposes can change the very nature of the information that is collected; if the subject of the study knows it is being observed and by whom, its behavior will change. That is the point of studying it anonymously. Moreover, not all automated data collection is abusive, and not all of it is used to train AI, but these proposed bills risk deterring archivists, researchers, and civic technologists from using automated data collection tools out of fear of liability. Journalists use scraping to analyze public records, as in the WSJ story. Researchers use it to study online discrimination and misinformation . The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has used crawlers to archive more than one trillion webpages, creating a historical record of the internet that would otherwise constantly change or disappear. That archival record has helped provide the factual background for thousands of news stories, evidence in hundreds of court cases across the country, and often simply a backup for when things go wrong. It is not just archivists who rely on scraping to advance the public good. Disability advocates have used scraping to automatically evaluate over one million websites to detect accessibility problems. Public health researchers use scraping to track the opioid epidemic as well as misinformation surrounding addiction and treatment. The federal government relies on crawlers to scan for threat detection, offering free cybersecurity services to organizations across the country. And for some of these users, anonymity is essential to the integrity and safety of their work. For example, environmental researchers gathering information from public corporate disclosures or satellite image portals may fear retaliation from the companies they are investigating. Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy Subscribe Loading... Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list. The First Amendment has historically protected us from government-imposed identification requirements tied to receiving information. In Lamont v. Postmaster General , the Supreme Court struck down a law requiring recipients to affirmatively identify themselves before receiving certain political publications. The same principle applies to web crawling: requiring people to identify themselves as a condition of accessing publicly available information burdens the freedom to receive information. That concern is heightened when laws use vague language. If researchers cannot easily understand what it means to “deploy” a crawler in a prohibited way, or what activity is “reasonably likely to burden or impair a website,” they may refrain from scraping rather than risk violating the law. As we wrote in our letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, “deanonymization threatens the core of the open web without actually addressing these technological and potential economic harms of AI-related crawling.” Unmasking a crawler does not reduce the number of requests it sends to a server. It does not compensate a publisher whose content is used to build an AI product. And it does not restore referral traffic that publishers may lose when users turn to an AI chatbot for information. Indeed, existing laws can be used to address many harmful uses of scraped data. For example, privacy laws can restrict how sensitive data is processed. Copyright law can respond to infringing AI-generated outputs. Consumer protection law can address deceptive data collection or use. To tackle the specific issues raised by aggressive AI scraping, policymakers could support the development of standardized, interoperable technical solutions to help websites better manage automated traffic. Standards bodies such as the Internet Engineering Task Force are exploring new protocols for managing machine access to online content and developing mechanisms for anonymous attestation of good crawler behavior. Policymakers should allow that work to develop rather than prematurely imposing legal and technical measures that harm “good” bots and that “bad” bots will quickly learn to evade. And if policymakers conclude that new legislation is necessary, liability should turn on conduct that causes identifiable harms like overwhelming servers with excessive requests, engaging in fraud, or collecting data for prohibited uses. The spread of AI crawling has created legitimate challenges for publishers and website operators requiring thoughtful policy responses. But policymakers should resist treating anonymity as something wrong in and of itself. The open web depends on the ability to access, analyze, and preserve publicly available information without revealing our identity and seeking permission from every website owner first. Policymakers who want to curb abusive crawling while preserving a healthy information ecosystem have better options, and we are eager to help them. We invite legislators at the state and federal levels to reach out to us about how alternative proposals could target harmful conduct while protecting the tools that journalists, researchers, archivists, and citizens have long used to navigate the digital world. Support Tech Policy Press If you've found our work helpful, consider supporting us. Donate Authors Lila Bailey Lila Bailey is Senior Policy Counsel for the Internet Archive, a 501(c)(3) non-profit research library that has collected 30 years of web history that it makes available to the public for free via the Wayback Machine. Tess Vartanian Tess Vartanian is a Legal Fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology. Her areas of focus include protecting internet users’ free expression rights, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, and fostering an open internet. title: Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man
body_text: Remembering Patrick Stewart: What Captain Picard taught us Skip to main content Sections Epaper Sports Red Sox Patriots Celtics Bruins High Schools Colleges Women's Sports TV & Radio Metro Weather Politics Transportation Education Cambridge & Somerville Around Mass. Newsletters More Print this Article View Comments Metro Weather Politics Sports Business Puzzles Rhode Island Globe Magazine Opinion Health care Arts Lifestyle Education Cambridge & Somerville Money, Power, Inequality Spotlight Technology Climate Cars Real Estate Events Appreciation Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man Print this Article View Comments Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. GLOBE PHOTO/ELLIOTT MARKS Patrick Stewart died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him. For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family. Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy. Two of the Globe’s dyed-in-the-wool Star Trek fans share what Captain Picard, and Patrick Stewart, meant to them. John Hilliard: For a younger, and likely wiser generation, stanning a bald middle-aged English actor who played a French guy on a spaceship may be a questionable life choice. But here is the thing: What made Stewart resonate as Picard was how he rooted the character, as in the best of fairy tales, in emotional truth. Jason Laughlin: I agree. Picard seemed as real as the complex characters that would start to populate prestige TV a decade later. But unlike anti-heroes such as Tony Soprano and Walter White, Stewart gave us a nuanced character we actually admired. He loved his job. He had passions like archaeology , Shakespeare , and music . He held to his ideals even when it meant terrible personal sacrifice. In the mess of American politics over the past 20 years, there have been so many times I’ve longed for a Picard-style speech that makes right and wrong crystal clear. “You know, there are some words I’ve known since I was a schoolboy,” Picard said when a Joe McCarthy-esque admiral began witch hunting on the Enterprise. “With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably.” His character’s moral clarity, and Stewart’s conviction in delivering it, put an end to the admiral’s reign of terror. If only real world oppression could be dispelled so easily. For decades, Patrick Stewart was a star of stage and screen, but no role defined him quite like the noble space captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek: The Next Generation. STEVE FORREST/NYT JH: Full disclosure : Star Trek is a show, which Youtube will prove, that leaned hard on latex foreheads and sometimes-flimsy production to tell stories of intergalactic scallywags known as Klingons and Borg, Romulans and Cardassians. Like free office coffee, it’s an acquired taste. JL: One of my friends has a theory that if you didn’t get into Star Trek before you’re 18 years old, you’re never really going to get it. To me, what’s so accessible, and radical, about Stewart, though, was his ability to convincingly portray vulnerability while still maintaining Picard as a credible leader. One episode saw Picard return to his home village in France to heal from a traumatic assault. At the conclusion, Stewart surrenders the control that was his character’s hallmark and falls into the mud, sobbing, over his failure to fight off his assailants. It’s a raw, real, depiction of a broken man. Stewart shifts from total collapse into slow recovery by reconciling with his brother. Grief is replaced by warmth, and Stewart sells it perfectly. JH: Totally. He knew how to make that show work for him. That’s despite an episode where he faces off against a giant, talking tar pit . Or the one where he sells eating a sandwich in the sci-fi version of the family station wagon. Or when he chugs Ecto Cooler (remember Ecto Cooler?) with a depressed Scotty , from the original Star Trek, and shares stories about first jobs and first girlfriends. He even shows up in tights, as discount Errol Flynn Robin Hood. As a kid raised on television before there was an Internet, Stewart plugged into a world where figures like Mr. Rogers and Bob Ross presented a model for manhood that was gentle, patient, and a teacher. Stewart played Picard in a similar vein, basically everyone’s Space Dad. Even as recently as last month, Captain Jean-Luc Picard appeared on Star Trek Day in the London Underground. Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for Paramount+ JL: This is embarrassing, but the first TV episode that moved me to tears was from The Next Generation. “ The Inner Light ” has Picard experience an entire lifetime as a different person on an alien planet. Again, the actor found his character’s humanity through slow revelation that perhaps a life with a wife and children is just as big an adventure as exploring space. “Seize the time,” Picard says to his daughter in this other life. “Live now! Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.” At the end of the episode, it’s revealed the decades he spent in that other life were an illusion he experienced in less than an hour. The only tangible thing he has from that world is a flute he learned to play in that other life. In the final moments, Picard plays it again, and without saying a word Stewart plays absolute heartbreak. Seeing a strong, confident leader who was able to express regrets, sadness, and heartache left a lasting impression. Well into his 80s, Patrick Stewart was playing the character he became best known for. Richard Shotwell/AP Photo/Richard Shotwell JH: Imagine you’re a kid watching TV, and you feel kind of alone, unsure of yourself. And then there’s Stewart, in full reassuring teaching mode. It’s the episode where Wil Wheaton’s character is struggling with tremendous guilt as he tries to hide his complicity in the death of a friend. Stewart, as Picard, is on to him. Wheaton’s character, Wesley Crusher, is as close to a son as Picard will likely ever have, and Stewart leans into Picard’s grief, grief from knowing that doing the right thing will likely destroy the younger man’s future. “A lie of omission is still a lie,” Picard tells Wheaton. Stewart’s voice cracks as Picard remembers meeting Wheaton’s character for the first time. He sat in Picard’s chair. He knew every button on the ship, every function. He was annoyed, Picard growls. Stewart pulls back. Picard never had any doubt that Crusher would grow up into an outstanding officer. Until that moment. “The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it’s scientific truth, or historical truth, or personal truth,” says Picard, who then delivers the gut punch. “If you can’t find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don’t deserve to wear that uniform.” It doesn’t matter if you know what a Starfleet is, or if someone can be an officer of one. Stewart always finds a way to connect his audience to the emotional truth. When you’re a kid, you’re looking for lessons, even if you don’t want to admit it. Stewart, as a master of navigating the human heart, understood the moment and his character. Ultimately, Picard was a teacher, and a guide, not just for the characters with whom he shared a scene, but for the audience as well. JL: Stewart was 47 when he began playing Picard. I’m just a year older than him now, and the very best of his episodes have taken on new resonance. Family tensions are real and devastating. Professional choices have lasting consequences. The melancholy of middle age lingers on the periphery of every happy moment. Patrick Stewart’s Picard still serves as a role model. He showed how to face those moments with dignity, optimism, and a belief in the enduring capacity to be our best selves. Jason Laughlin can be reached at jason.laughlin@globe.com . Follow him @jasmlaughlin . John Hilliard can be reached at john.hilliard@globe.com or on Signal at john_hilliard.70. Follow him on Bluesky at iamjohnhilliard.bsky.social. Dismiss alert {{ message }} chris124567 cfsolve Repository navigation Code Issues Pull requests 3 ( 3 ) Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items cfsolve Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 49 ( 49 ) Star 457 ( 457 ) You must be signed in to star a repository About Cloudflare turnstile and challenge page solver in Rust (full reverse, request based) Resources Readme MIT license Activity Stars 457 stars Watchers 0 watching Forks 49 forks Report repository master Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 7 Commits 7 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date examples examples profiles profiles src src vendor vendor .gitignore .gitignore Cargo.lock Cargo.lock Cargo.toml Cargo.toml LICENSE LICENSE README.md README.md rust-toolchain.toml rust-toolchain.toml rustfmt.toml rustfmt.toml View all files Repository files navigation README MIT license More items cfsolve cfsolve is a Rust library and command line tool that solves Cloudflare Turnstile widgets and challenge pages without a headless browser. It returns a Turnstile token for widgets or a cf_clearance cookie for challenge pages. Turnstile widgets can be solved using the page URL, the sitekey, and optionally the page's HTML (this should not be required in most cases). Challenge pages require a direct fetch or the HTML of the page. Browser profiles cfsolve impersonates a specific browser, described by a profile file. One is included: profiles/safari-26-ios.json (Safari on iPhone). Each profile references recorded responses to the challenge's browser checks, stored as JSON in a directory. Keep each profile with its directory when you copy. Producing these files requires some manual (or AI) effort though it can be greatly aided by solving challenges in a real web browser with the proxy set to the address of a running capture-proxy , which records the decoded payloads sent to Cloudflare. Currently only Safari and Chrome(ium) profile types are supported. Building You need the Rust version pinned in rust-toolchain.toml , plus CMake, a C/C++ compiler, libclang, and Git (to patch and build BoringSSL). cargo build --release --bin challenge Command line tool ./target/release/challenge --page ' https://example.com/login ' /tmp/solve \ --solve --fingerprint profiles/safari-26-ios.json On success it prints the token (or cf_clearance=... ) and sends progress to stderr. The directory argument holds all requests and responses for debugging, so it must be empty or not exist yet. By default it solves the first Turnstile widget on the page, or clears the challenge page. To pick one widget when the page has several, pass its sitekey, with its action and cData when the site sets them. With --sitekey , it fails on a challenge page. ./target/release/challenge --page ' https://example.com/login ' /tmp/solve \ --solve --fingerprint profiles/safari-26-ios.json \ --sitekey ' SITEKEY ' --action ' login ' --cdata ' CUSTOM_DATA ' If you only have a sitekey, add --blank-page and set --page to the site's real URL. Option Description --fingerprint <file> Browser profile file to use. Required. --page <url> The page with the widget, or the challenge page. --solve Solve the widget or challenge. Without this, cfsolve stops after sending the widget's first payload. --sitekey <key> Select a widget by sitekey. --action <value> , --cdata <value> Override the widget's action and cData. This needs --sitekey . --blank-page Skip loading the page. Render the widget on a blank page at the page URL. This needs --solve and --sitekey . --proxy <url> Send every request through an http:// , https:// , socks5:// , or socks5h:// proxy. Put credentials in the URL, as in socks5h://user:password@host:1080 . -h , --help Show help. Library Add cfsolve as a path dependency and copy its [patch] section, since Cargo only reads patches from the top-level Cargo.toml : [ dependencies ] cfsolve = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve " , default-features = false } tokio = { version = " 1 " , features = [ " macros " , " rt-multi-thread " ] } [ patch . crates-io ] btls-sys = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/btls-sys " } wreq = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/wreq " } http2 = { path = " /path/to/cfsolve/vendor/http2 " } default-features = false turns off the internal tools so only the solver remains. Use the Rust version in rust-toolchain.toml or newer. use cfsolve :: { Browser , Options , PageSource , Turnstile } ; # [ tokio :: main ] async fn main ( ) -> Result < ( ) , Box < dyn std :: error :: Error > > { let browser = Browser :: read ( "/path/to/cfsolve/profiles/safari-26-ios.json" ) ? ; let options = Options :: default ( ) ; let turnstile = Turnstile { url : "https://example.com/login" . parse ( ) ? , page : PageSource :: Navigate , widget : None , } ; let token = browser . solve_turnstile ( turnstile , & options ) . await ? ; println ! ( "{token}" ) ; let cleared = browser . clear ( & "https://example.com/" . parse ( ) ? , & options ) . await ? ; println ! ( "cf_clearance={}" , cleared . clearance ) ; println ! ( "{} cookies; protected page: {}" , cleared . cookies . len ( ) , cleared . page . url ) ; Ok ( ( ) ) } Load a Browser once and share it. Concurrent operations each get their own connections and cookies. Send the cf_clearance cookie from the same IP address and user agent as the profile, or Cloudflare will reject it. Turnstile with a sitekey or your own HTML PageSource::Navigate fetches the page. With only a URL and sitekey, use PageSource::Blank and specify the widget: use cfsolve :: { PageSource , Turnstile , Widget } ; let turnstile = Turnstile { url : "https://example.com/login" . parse ( ) ? , page : PageSource :: Blank , widget : Some ( Widget { sitekey : "SITEKEY" . into ( ) , action : Some ( "login" . into ( ) ) , cdata : None , } ) , } ; let token = browser . solve_turnstile ( turnstile , & options ) . await ? ; Set action and cdata to the values the site uses, or None when the site doesn't set them. You can also pass a Widget with PageSource::Navigate to pick one widget out of several or to supply one the site adds with JavaScript. For a page you have already loaded, such as one behind a login, pass its URL and HTML: PageSource :: Html { html : std :: fs :: read_to_string ( "account.html" ) ? , referrer_policy : None , // Or the response's Referrer-Policy header. } The widget runs in a cross-site iframe, so you don't need your login cookies. With Html , widget: None solves the first widget on the page, while Blank always needs a Widget and renders it on a blank page at the site's URL. Challenge pages browser.clear(&url, &options) fetches the page and clears the challenge. The Clearance it returns contains the cf_clearance cookie, all cookies for the page, and the protected page. It fails with Error::NotChallenged when there's no challenge. If you fetched the challenge page yourself, pass the response as a FetchedPage to browser.clear_fetched(page, &options) . Use the same IP and user agent as the profile. If you don't know whether a URL shows a widget or a challenge page, use browser.solve , which covers both cases: use cfsolve :: Outcome ; match browser . solve ( & url , & options ) . await ? { Outcome :: Token ( token ) => println ! ( "{token}" ) , Outcome :: Cleared ( cleared ) => println ! ( "cf_clearance={}" , cleared . clearance ) , } Options Set a proxy per operation through Options , using HTTP, HTTPS, or SOCKS5: let options = cfsolve :: Options { proxy : Some ( "socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080" . into ( ) ) , .. Default :: default ( ) } ; Library operations are silent by default. For progress messages and debug files, implement Sink and set options.sink to Some(Arc::new(your_sink)) . Errors Error Cause Retry? Error::Network Connection failed. Yes Error::Rejected Cloudflare rejected the solution. Yes Error::Blocked The site returned an error page instead of a challenge. No Error::Challenged You asked for a Turnstile token but got a challenge page. Yes, after clearing it Error::NotChallenged You asked for a challenge clearance but there was no challenge. No Error::Config Invalid profile or options. No Error::Unsupported Any other failure, such as a new challenge build or a page with no widget. title: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code
body_text: Cisco is letting a 27-year-old refactor 98% of its legacy code with unlimited AI tokens: ‘Go nuts’ | Fortune Search Subscribe Home Latest Fortune 500 Finance Tech Leadership Lifestyle Rankings Multimedia Trending now 1 The Pentagon and Britain are bracing for the power to go out. The ultrawealthy got there first, with backup generators, escape homes, and stockpiles 2 ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem 3 Jeff Bezos once gave Eva Longoria and the admiral behind Osama bin Laden's capture $100 million—but she says you don't need wealth to give back 1 The Pentagon and Britain are bracing for the power to go out. The ultrawealthy got there first, with backup generators, escape homes, and stockpiles 2 ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem 3 Jeff Bezos once gave Eva Longoria and the admiral behind Osama bin Laden's capture $100 million—but she says you don't need wealth to give back Success Gen Z Cisco chief found a 27-year-old ex-founder ‘buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic’—now he’s upgrading 98% of its code By Orianna Rosa Royle Orianna Rosa Royle Associate Editor, Success Down Arrow Button Icon By Orianna Rosa Royle Orianna Rosa Royle Associate Editor, Success Down Arrow Button Icon October 30, 2026, 3:00 AM ET Meet Paddy, the 27-year-old Cisco’s president calls an “energizer bunny.” The Gen Z ex-founder has been given unlimited AI tokens and told to “go nuts.” Getty Images Google source logo Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing ; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free . Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him. Recommended Video “I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.” The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs , the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.” That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way. So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months. Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.” Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem. “If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said. Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask. And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point. “Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.” “What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.” And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.” His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up. He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?” She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack. “I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her. Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset. Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience. When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.” And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI , which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation. These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.” Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo , Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience. “I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune . “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.” And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla , OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment. Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford. “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune . “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.” And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI. “The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.” “Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here. title: Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated
body_text: Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our times | Poetry | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 1 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world An orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc. Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images View image in fullscreen An orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc. Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images Book of the day Poetry Review Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our times The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de force Philip Terry Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he poet laureate is paid a salary of £5,750 per annum plus a barrel of sherry. No specific duties are attached to the role, but there is an expectation that poets will write verse for public occasions and royal events, a duty that Simon Armitage has fulfilled by writing a poem on the death of Elizabeth II, Floral Tribute, and another to mark the coronation of Charles and Camilla in 2023. Though it’s an awkward time for the royals, no laureate is going to write about them behaving badly (it wasn’t John Dryden, the first laureate, who wrote about Charles II’s bedroom habits, but John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester). And yet with Gilgamesh, Armitage does deliver a poem about royalty’s misdeeds, at least in part. The epic originated in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) at least 4,000 years ago, and it begins with the eponymous demigod, king of Uruk, lording it over his subjects. Among other bad habits, he exercises the “right of the first night”, which allows him to bed newlywed brides before their husbands. To check his powers, the gods create his counterpart, the wild man Enkidu, who confronts Gilgamesh outside the house of one of these brides. The two rivals turned comrades then embark on a series of extraordinary adventures, including battles with Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, and with the winged Bull of Heaven, sent by the goddess Ishtar in revenge after Gilgamesh rejects her marriage proposal. Following Enkidu’s death, Gilgamesh sets out alone on a desperate quest for immortality that leads him to the very edge of the world. In his introduction Armitage draws our attention to the poem’s rich modern resonance, including its frankness about sex workers, who play a key role in bringing Enkidu to Uruk, its ecological dimension – Enkidu’s death is a punishment for cutting down the forest guarded by Humbaba – and the way the relationship of Gilgamesh and Enkidu can be seen as a celebration of same-sex physical love (Gilgamesh loves his companion “like a wife”). Most striking of all is the way the heroes’ fight with Humbaba echoes modern resource wars. The Gulf wars took place in the same geographical region, though the commodity in question was not timber – the prime building material at the time of the poem – but oil. double quotation mark Some of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touch The poem’s uniquely fragmented history makes it both ancient and modern. Sumerian sources date back to 2000BC, but it remained lost until fragments of cuneiform tablets in a later Akkadian form were discovered by archaeologists in the 19th century. A tablet on display in the British Museum drew the attention of George Smith, employed by a firm that designed bank notes, and he repeatedly visited the museum in his lunch hour to gaze at it. When the keeper of Babylonian antiquities asked him what he was doing, Smith replied that he was reading it. Later, now in the employ of the British Museum, Smith was excited to discover a tablet describing a great flood. Crying “I am the first person to read that after 2000 years of oblivion,” he rushed about the room in a state of great excitation, and to the astonishment of those present began to undress. The passage Smith had deciphered comes towards the end of the poem, where Gilgamesh visits the now-immortal flood survivor Uta-napishtim – the poem’s Noah character – in an attempt to find immortality himself. It caused a sensation in Victorian England because of its similarity to the flood story in the Book of Genesis: here perhaps was evidence of the historical veracity of the event. This fragmented history of the poem is reflected in the way it has come down to us in broken tablet form, which Armitage compares to a vast jigsaw with pieces still missing. Readers who see this fragmentation as integral to the poem may be disappointed with Armitage’s approach, which is generally to paper over the cracks, as he puts it (though he does present passages that have been restored from later sources in prose, and occasionally leaves gaps whose contents he speculates on in detailed footnotes). One feature Armitage is very faithful to is the incantatory use of repetition, as in the journey to meet Humbaba – “After forty leagues they stopped and broke bread. / After sixty leagues they stopped and pitched camp” – which he says “enacts the mundane regularity of a long slog across featureless terrain”. Generally, the results are fresh and impressive, as in the poem’s opening lines, as solid as the rock they were once carved on: He witnessed great depths, saw the land’s bedrock. Astute in all subjects, wise in every matter, Gilgamesh glimpsed the foundations of life. Nothing escaped him; he possessed all knowledge, had learned each discipline in equal measure, understood completely the ways of the world. He uncovered secrets, revealed what was hidden, brought back word from before the Great Flood, trudged distant paths, earned his rest. He carved his trials and travails in a stone. Armitage wisely avoids rhyme, unlike some recent versions – there is no evidence of rhyme in the original text – but he knits his poem together tightly with a standard four-beat line, a fine-spun mixture of the modern and the archaic, and a smattering of the alliteration he employed in his translation of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight . Some of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touch – Gilgamesh’s mother Ninsun, “She-Wild-Cow”, purifies herself with “tamarisk and soapwort”. Others have a delicious contemporaneity, as Humbaba calls Enkidu, created by the gods out of a lump of clay, a “half-wit”, a “crossbred freak” who “never sucked milk from his mother’s tit”. Of all the scenes, it is those in the forest, as the heroes make their way towards the home of Humbaba, that bring out Armitage’s best poetry, which sings and clatters its way through the undergrowth: The canopy was knitted and knotted with creepers; sap and resin came raining down and flowed away through channels and gorges. A bird called out, then the forest echoed with the racket of more birds calling in answer. A lone cicada sounded its note, triggering a chorus of piping and hymning. A turtle dove answered the cries of a pigeon . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Bookmarks Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion The register of Gilgamesh remains one of the great unknowns of the poem. Given the nature of its content – often violent, mocking and sexually explicit – there is no reason to assume it should, as it generally is, be translated into elevated language. Armitage tackles this head on by mixing different registers and idiolects. His tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings, and it is likely to become one of the standard renditions in English. It cannot, though, be the last word on this continuingly resonant poem, whose fragments are still coming to light in museum collections, fresh excavations and accidental finds. Philip Terry is the author of Dictator: A Free Version of the Epic of Gilgamesh in Globish (Carcanet, £12.99). Gilgamesh: A New Verse Translation by Simon Armitage is published by Faber (£14.99).
