title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
body_text: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. Observability Real Talk Subscribe Sign in AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them. When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Elizabeth Feb 28, 2026 29 6 5 Share 💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz! This newsletter is a n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between! & This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚 Subscribe There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days. The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering , that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027. Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters? Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient. The Ironies of Automation: Part-I Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉). In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation . It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today. Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for. Ring any bells yet? 🙂 Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems. The exact problems that require deep expertise , the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising. Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing. Current State of AI in SRE Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering. What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted? Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today. What’s on the horizon? Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks. PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model. Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated. Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation. Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context. But here’s the catch. If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down. Subscribe if you wish to read some more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe The Crisis of Deskilling This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture. In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill. In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect. Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always . My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust . We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening . It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied. For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated. But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling . Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing. The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing . SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult. What Can We Do About It? We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward. A few approaches worth considering: Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities . This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged. Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture. The Bigger Picture Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply. We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz . We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product. Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned. One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would. And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure. The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts. Here’s the LinkedIn post our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this. Thanks for reading Observability Real Talk! Subscribe if you wish to read more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones! Subscribe 29 6 5 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Tim 1d The US navy also went through this 50+ years ago. They had the ability to automate nearly everything, but the admiral in charge of the project wisely said that a machine could suggest what to do, but there must always be a human in the loop to actually carry out the action, or we would lose our ability when the machines failed. Reply Share Piotr Zakrzewski 16h Also in novel incidents you are not left on your own with just your (rusty) skills. It is still AI plus you, even if AI cannot solve it on its own, you can still iterate during the incident, making observations, using AI to ask questions and dissecting the problem to eliminate root cause candidates. This is how it goes for me at my job. I am much more confident going into a SEV response knowing I have well integrated AI on my side. Reply Share 4 more comments... I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original. This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life. What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Try it in your browser . The playground sets a page as a printer's proof, grows its margin with the same Lua, and hands it back as an SVG, a LaTeX preamble or a Typst page setup. Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free. Two documents share one package, and two more ( showcase.tex , spread.tex ) show what else it does: florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex composition authored : stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown : a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page preview Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn. Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below. 300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems. Watch it grow as it grows with the free space it fills Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives. The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way ( build/grow-6.gif and .mp4 , about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles. The margin reads the text showcase.tex , "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows. The grown margin can respond to the document around it: Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". Flowers at the headings. With the option sections , every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. Seasons. With the option aging , the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead. One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where. Visitors Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out. Any ink The whole palette comes from one color, ink : Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray. Themes Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric , and with theme=math . The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, theme-<name>.lua , that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own. theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes ( theme-geometric.lua ). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page. theme=math is no plant at all ( theme-math.lua , drawing from figures.lua ): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families , figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is. \usepackage [ grown,theme=geometric ]{ florilegium } % or theme=math; the whole document \florilegiumtheme {math} % or from the page this stands on A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed. Less in the margin Seed 6 at density=1 , 0.5 , 0.2 and 0.05 , and at intensity=0.5 . A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme: density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things. intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail. \usepackage [ grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6 ]{ florilegium } At the defaults ( 1 and 1 ) every page is exactly the page it was before. One ornament in the text Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one. \usepackage [ nomargin ]{ florilegium } % ornaments only, no garden in the margin \florilegiumornament {leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf. \florilegiumornament [size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower} Any primitive works ( leaf , leaflet , flower , blossom , bud , bell , lily , cyme , umbel , butterfly , bee , bird , hedera , sparkle , ...), and so do the current theme's ( crystal with geometric ; knot , polyhedron , koch , ... with math ). Both sides of the page spread.tex , pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme. The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document ( twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left. SVG, Typst and the browser The playground , seed 12 in autumn on a last page. The page is a proof, and its colophon, the note a book keeps about its paper, ink and printing, is the set of controls: every copper word in it can be changed. The same Lua can draw a page without TeX. svg.lua runs the package's own code with a small stand-in for the few parts of TeX it touches (the page's lengths, the page number, and the node a drawing goes into), takes the PDF drawing commands that ink.lua writes as it always does, and rewrites them as SVG. Nothing in the drawing code changes, so the garden is the one LuaLaTeX would draw, not an imitation of it. texlua svg.lua --seed 7 > margin.svg # page 1 of a document with \def\florilegiumseed{7} lua svg.lua --seed 7 --season autumn --ink 5B2A1F --left 25mm --right 65mm > margin.svg texlua svg.lua --help # paper, margins, two-sided pages, the last page, themes... make svg SEED=7 # -> build/svg-7.svg Any Lua 5.3 or 5.4 runs it. Lengths are read the way TeX reads them and colors are converted the way xcolor converts them, so --seed 7 with the default margins gives, byte for byte, the drawing on page 1 of florilegium-grow.tex built with seed 7. The SVG is a whole page with a transparent background, which makes it a page background anywhere. In Typst: # set page ( paper : " a4 " , margin : ( left : 68mm , right : 22mm , top : 32mm , bottom : 30mm ), background : image ( " margin.svg " , width : 100% , height : 100% )) The playground runs the same files in the browser with wasmoon , Lua 5.4 compiled to WebAssembly, in a background worker, and a page grows in about a second. Seed 7 there is seed 7 here. The proof is the control surface as much as the colophon is: the measure above it sets the margin, and dragging the foot of the text up makes a last page. The text on the proof describes the garden that just grew, from the counts the growth loop keeps. Under it, the page can be seen as readers with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia see it, with the distance between the ink and the accent measured for each (Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes's model, distances in Oklab); a pairing that is hard to tell apart is flagged when you choose it. Next to the download are the LaTeX preamble, the Typst setup and the command line that make the same garden, and the address bar keeps every setting, so a garden can be shared as a link. To run it from a clone, serve the repository with make playground and open http://localhost:8000/web/ . The math theme works too. Its figures come from the same Lua; its equations and symbols, which TeX sets in a PDF, are set in the playground by MathJax in the same Computer Modern, and the command line leaves them out. The fonts are served with the page (IM FELL DW Pica, and Latin Modern renamed as its license asks), so nothing is fetched from a font service. In PostScript postscript/florilegium.ps : the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how. The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua , flora.lua and grow.lua , procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file: gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden -dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map: Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end. Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY . Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition. The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps , with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency. Build LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex , whose seasons need the page count). make # the four PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* make svg SEED=7 # the same page as SVG, without TeX -> build/svg-7.svg make playground # the browser playground at http://localhost:8000/web/ No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it: docker build -t florilegium-tex tools make RUN=tools/in-docker Or paste florilegium.sty , the .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX. Use it in your own document: \usepackage [ grown ]{ florilegium } % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math, % density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6 % two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin \definecolor {ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor {accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ... \florilegiuminitial [4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T. ... a flower in the margin beside this line \florilegiumbloom ... \florilegiumage {0.8} % grown only: autumn from here on \florilegiumtheme {geometric} % another theme, from the page this stands on \florilegiumornament {leaf} % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter \florilegiumtextend % grown only: at the very end of the text A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}" . Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale: \begin { tikzpicture } \begin { scope }[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20] \florilegiumdraw {flower}{1.3} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(5,0)}] \florilegiumdraw {leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(8,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}} \end { scope } \begin { scope }[shift={(11,1)}] \florilegiumdraw {butterfly}{1.5} \end { scope } \end { tikzpicture } With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex ), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math . How it works Drawing ( ink.lua ). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink : navy to mist at the hue of ink , interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons. Primitives ( flora.lua ). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost. Authored composition ( authored.lua ). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root. Grown composition ( grow.lua ), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with \pagetotal in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation. Reading the page ( florilegium.lua ). A heading or \florilegiumbloom leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink. Initials ( initial.lua ). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper. Procedural ≠ random. The seed is derived from the page number, so page n always gets garden n . Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset. See CLAUDE.md for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done. Credits The Reddit post that asked the question (see Origin ). The growth loop follows Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The tone ramp is computed in Oklab , Björn Ottosson's perceptual color space; the conversion matrices in ink.lua are his, released into the public domain. The random numbers come from mulberry32 , Tommy Ettinger's public-domain generator. \florilegiumornament , its ink and seed=random keys, and the density option answer issue #4 from rubyFeedback. The playground runs the Lua in the browser with wasmoon (MIT) and typesets the math theme's equations with MathJax (Apache 2.0), both loaded from jsDelivr. It is set in Igino Marini's IM FELL DW Pica (SIL OFL) and Latin Modern (GUST e-foundry, GUST Font License); see web/fonts/README.md . Its color-blindness views use the model of Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes, A Physiologically-based Model for Simulation of Color Vision Deficiency (IEEE TVCG, 2009). The math theme's figures keep the names of the people they come from: Maurer's roses, Vogel's model of the sunflower, Temple Fay's butterfly curve, the Petersen graph, Koch's snowflake, Hilbert's curve, Lissajous figures, the gasket of Apollonius. It displays the real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations, and more, all within your terminal—no telescope required! Configure sky views by date, time, and location with precise ASCII-rendered visuals. See usage for all supported options! astroterm is constantly improving, and we'd love to hear your ideas! If you have a suggestion or find a bug, please open an issue and share your feedback. See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines on building, testing, and contributing to astroterm . The night sky above Singapore on January 2, 2025 See usage on how to obtain this view Table of Contents 🌌 astroterm Features Installation Usage Troubleshooting Citations Data Sources Features 🔭 Highly Customizable: Choose any date, time, and location to explore past, present, or future celestial events 📐 Accurate Rendering: View the moon, stars, and planets with as much precision as terminal graphics allow 🌘 Moon Phases: Precise lunar phases in real-time 🌌 Constellation Figures: Detailed constellation shapes ⚡ Performance Optimized: Lightweight and fast ASCII rendering Stars over Sydney, Australia on January 6, 2025 Installation Several installation methods are provided based on your platform. If none of these fit your needs, you can always build from source . Refer to troubleshooting for help resolving any issues. Arch Linux You can install astroterm from the extra repository using pacman : pacman -S astroterm Fedora You can install astroterm directly from the Fedora package repository on Fedora 40+. sudo dnf install astroterm Homebrew You can install astroterm from Homebrew via: brew install astroterm Nix You can try the package in a temporary environment with the following command: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command astroterm Argument flags are added by wrapping the command in quotes. For example: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command " astroterm -u -c " To make astroterm available from your $PATH , add it to your configuration.nix: environment.systemPackages = with pkgs ; [ ... astroterm ] Guix You can install astroterm directly from the Guix main channel starting from this commit . guix time-machine --commit=4b5f0408e66392ab745dc0f7830732217d88f17d -- shell astroterm Or after guix pull : guix shell astroterm -- astroterm --help # to try guix package --install astroterm # add to current profile Prebuilt Executable Unix Download the latest executable using wget wget -O astroterm " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-<os>-<arch> " Replace <os> with the appropriate platform: Linux: linux macOS: darwin Replace <arch> with the appropriate architecture: Linux: x86_64 (arm64 support to come after Ubuntu arm64 runners are available) Apple Silicon (M-series): aarch64 Intel-based Macs: x86_64 To view all supported combinations, see the Releases page. Run the executable chmod +x ./astroterm ./astroterm Windows Download the latest .exe file using PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest : Invoke-WebRequest - Uri " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-win-x86_64.exe " - OutFile " astroterm.exe " Run the .exe .\ astroterm.exe Building From Source Usage Options The --help flag displays all supported options: Usage: astroterm [OPTION]... -a, --latitude=<degrees> Observer latitude [-90°, 90°] (default: 0.0) -o, --longitude=<degrees> Observer longitude [-180°, 180°] (default: 0.0) -d, --datetime=<yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ss> Observation datetime in UTC -t, --threshold=<float> Only render stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 5.0) -l, --label-thresh=<float> Label stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 0.25) -f, --fps=<int> Frames per second (default: 24) -s, --speed=<float> Animation speed multiplier (default: 1.0) -c, --color Enable terminal colors -C, --constellations Draw constellation stick figures. Note: a constellation is only drawn if all stars in the figure are over the threshold -g, --grid Draw an azimuthal grid -u, --unicode Use unicode characters -b, --braille Use braille characters for constellation lines (requires Unicode) -q, --quit-on-any Quit on any keypress (default is to quit on 'q' or 'ESC' only) -m, --metadata Display metadata -r, --aspect-ratio=<float> Override the calculated terminal cell aspect ratio. Use this if your projection is not 'square.' A value around 2.0 works well for most cases -h, --help Print this help message -B, --bash-completions Print bash completions -i, --city=<city_name> Use the latitude and longitude of the provided city. If the name contains multiple words, enclose the name in single or double quotes. For a list of available cities, see: https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/blob/main/data/ cities.csv -v, --version Display version info and exit Shell Completions To enable Tab completions in Bash, add the following line to your ~/.bashrc : source <( astroterm --bash-completions ) Example 1 To achieve the "spinning globe" effect as shown in the README GIF , use the following flags: astroterm --color --constellations --speed 10000 --fps 64 --city Singapore or astroterm -cC -s 10000 -f 64 -i Singapore for short. In fact, any city around the equator will work. Locations closer to the poles will look different because the apparent motion of the stars is more circular around the celestial pole rather than sweeping across the sky. Example 2 Say we wanted to view the sky at 5:00 AM (Eastern) on July 16, 1969—the morning of the Apollo 11 launch at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. We would run: astroterm --latitude 28.573469 --longitude -80.651070 --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 Finding the precise coordinates can be cumbersome, so we could also use the nearest major city to achieve a similar result: astroterm --city Orlando --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 -m While we're still waiting for someone to invent time travel, we can cheat a little by using Stellarium to confirm that this aligns with reality. If we then wanted to display constellations and add color, we would add --constellations --color as options. If you simply want the current time, don't specify the --datetime option and astroterm will use the system time. For your current location, you will still have to specify the --lat and --long options, or provide the nearest city with the --city option. For more options and help, run astroterm -h or astroterm --help . Tip Use a tool like LatLong to get your latitude and longitude. Tip Star magnitudes decrease as apparent brightness increases, i.e., to show more stars, increase the threshold. Troubleshooting Release Won't Download via Curl For some reason, curl does not follow the latest release redirect. Use wget to download the latest release or hardcode the tag in the link using curl . Or, just download via the releases page . Broken Unicode on Linux If Unicode characters do not display correctly in the terminal, you may need to configure your system's locale to support Unicode. Temporarily set the locale (add this to ~/.bashrc or equivalent to permanently enforce) export LC_ALL= " en_US.UTF-8 " export LC_CTYPE= " en_US.UTF-8 " Install and configure locales (example for Ubuntu/Debian) sudo apt update sudo apt install -y locales sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales During configuration, select en_US.UTF-8 as the default locale. Dismiss alert {{ message }} dbreunig nesformer Repository navigation Code Issues Pull requests Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items nesformer Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 8 ( 8 ) Star 243 ( 243 ) You must be signed in to star a repository About An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model Resources Readme License, License licenses found Activity Stars 243 stars Watchers 0 watching Forks 8 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 1 Commit 1 Commit Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date chipformer chipformer examples examples nesformer nesformer roms roms tests tests weights weights .gitignore .gitignore LICENSE LICENSE LICENSE.chipformer LICENSE.chipformer README.md README.md nesformer-weights.zip nesformer-weights.zip pyproject.toml pyproject.toml View all files Repository files navigation README License License More items nesformer An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model. The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt. nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal , which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory. Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level) Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked ). Quick start 1. Folder layout Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it: nesformer/ <- run commands from here ├── nesformer/ <- the Python package ├── chipformer/ <- Qwenputer's compiler ├── roms/ <- test ROMs (put your own here too) ├── examples/ <- sample GIFs and frame sheets ├── tests/ ├── LICENSE ├── LICENSE.chipformer ├── README.md ├── pyproject.toml └── weights/ <- from nesformer-weights.zip ├── config.json ├── generation_config.json ├── model.safetensors ├── nesformer.json └── SHA256SUMS The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere, pass --weights /path/to/weights to run , check or trace , or give the path to info . To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the top folder. 2. Install You need Python 3.11 or newer. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install numpy scipy numba pillow 3. Play a game python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593 " --show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif ) in the current folder. Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba. After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around 25 minutes. Playing your own ROMs Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely licensed test ROMs in roms/ . python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555 " That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations . Controller scripts --buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined by + , then @ , then one or more frame ranges joined by + : start@60-65 press Start during frames 60 to 65 right@200-600 hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600 a@250-265+300-315 press A twice right+b@200-600 hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.) The buttons are a , b , select , start , up , down , left and right . Frames count from power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer A press makes a higher jump. Commands Command What it does python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens) python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds) python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint Options for run : Option Default Meaning --frames N 120 Stop after N frames --buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above) --show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal) --gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF --png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both. --every N 1 Keep every N-th frame --scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times --engine fast fast (numba), numpy , or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s) --no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames) --max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens --trace FILE none Save the token ids run , check and trace all accept --weights , --engine , --buttons and --no-skip . check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/ . How it works What's in the weights, and what isn't In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host ( nesformer/host.py ) The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette 2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored) 32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace. The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows. The checkpoint weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code. Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM , with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216) Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs Hidden size 768 Vocabulary 263,808 tokens Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero , so the weights zip to 3.3 MB nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily. Layer plan Layer Attention (state) MLP 1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y 2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2 3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target 4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores 5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode 6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets 7 — the next token The trace Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it. As in Qwenputer's RISC-V core, the PC is implied rather than written: each final token carries its instruction's length, three DeltaNet counters tally the instructions of each length since the last jump, and the PC is the jump target plus that offset. Excerpts from Full Game: SEI P(000100 px0 L1) LDX #$40 X($40 c0 v0 px0 L2) STX $4017 IOW($4017=$40 L3) TXS S($FF L1) BIT $2002 IOR($2002) IN($00) P(000110 px0 L3) <- the host injects IN BPL $8017 J($8017) JSR $8279 PSH($FE) PSH($FD) J($8279) <- the return address is pushed in-circuit RTS PUL($FC) LO($7B) PUL($FD) J($827C) STA ($72),Y LO($08) HI($03) ST($00 a7=0 L2) <- pointer bytes latched, then the store STA $4014 IOW($4014=$02 L0) DM(0:$FF) … DM(255:$00) NT(L3) <- OAM DMA Most instructions take a single token; real game code averages 1.1–1.3 tokens per instruction. nesformer/spec.py documents every token family. How it was checked The reference CPU ( nesformer/cpu.py ) matches nestest's golden log for 3,348 instructions, and the py65 emulator on 5.7 million instructions of game code. The exact circuit , run in Qwenputer's evaluator with its bf16 exactness checks, predicts every reference token: all of nestest plus 283,610 positions of two games' boot sequences. The checkpoint in stock transformers (bf16, CPU) predicts 2,651 positions of nestest and Full Game with no mismatches. The weights, free-running , generate traces identical to the reference CPU's: Run Tokens Frames NES time Result nestest (official opcodes) 4,586 — — identical, ending in the expected HALT Thwaite, check 700,000 271 4.5 s identical trace and frames Thwaite, run 1,916,527 600 10.0 s all 300 saved frames match Full Game, run 2,645,885 420 7.0 s all 210 saved frames match The idle-loop skip changes nothing visible: frames and I/O writes, cycle timestamps included, match a run without it. Speed The default engine computes Qwen3.5's forward pass from model.safetensors , compiled with numba and skipping the all-zero blocks. It ran at about 1,650 tokens/s on one CPU core of the machine it was built on. The plain numpy engine does about 210, and stock transformers about 10. A real NES would need about 700,000 tokens per second. Games spend most of each frame in a loop that waits for vblank. When the host sees a loop body repeat exactly, with no RAM or I/O writes, it advances the clock to just before the next PPU event, and the remaining iterations still run. That cuts the token count by 2.6× to 4.2×. Overall, nesformer runs 150–290× slower than the real console. Limitations NROM cartridges only (iNES mapper 0). The CPU can address only 32 KB of program ROM at a time. Bigger games carry a bank-switching chip (a mapper , such as MMC1 or MMC3) that swaps which part of the ROM the CPU sees. nesformer's ROM reads happen inside the model, from a fixed 32 KB table, so it can't follow a bank switch yet. Supporting a mapper means storing the whole ROM in the state, keeping the bank registers there too, and adding one stage that turns each CPU address into a ROM address. Official opcodes only. An unofficial opcode emits HALT . Code must run from the cartridge ROM. A jump into RAM emits HALT . No IRQs (APU frame IRQ, DMC). BRK and NMI work. Read-modify-write instructions on I/O registers don't produce an I/O write, and $4020–$7FFF reads as 0 (no PRG-RAM). The PPU and APU aren't in the weights. The PPU renders one scanline at a time, so mid-scanline effects aren't reproduced. Sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there's no sound. Tests pip install pytest py65 python -m pytest -q tests The tests take a few minutes. They check the reference CPU against nestest's log, the circuit against the reference, the weights free-running against the reference, and the idle-loop skip. Running the checkpoint in stock transformers pip install " torch>=2.6 " " transformers>=5.22 " python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 3 --engine hf nesformer/hfcheck.py shows the whole procedure: load the checkpoint, decode one padding token, write the machine's state into the cache's DeltaNet states, then feed tokens one at a time. Files Path Contents nesformer/spec.py token families and records nesformer/cpu.py the reference 6502 that writes the trace nesformer/host.py everything around the CPU: PPU, controllers, NMI timing, cycle counting, idle skip nesformer/core.py the circuit and the state snapshot nesformer/weights.py the emitter that turns the circuit into a Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint nesformer/engine.py , fastengine.py run the weights (numpy / numba) nesformer/hfcheck.py run the weights in stock transformers nesformer/run.py , check.py , cli.py , __main__.py drivers, the teacher-forced check, the CLI chipformer/ Qwenputer's q35 compiler ( q35/ emitter and primitives, dsl/ graph) weights/ the compiled checkpoint and its SHA-256 checksum roms/ test ROMs; roms/SOURCES.md lists their authors and licenses examples/ GIFs and frame sheets from the runs; demo.gif is the Super Mario Bros. run shown at the top tests/test_nesformer.py the test suite Credits Qwenputer and its chipformer compiler: MIT, © 2026 Divyansh Agrawal ( LICENSE.chipformer ). That license also covers the code adapted from Qwenputer in nesformer/core.py and nesformer/weights.py . Its last paragraph refers to Qwenputer's CHIP-8 ROMs, which this repository does not include. Test ROMs: nestest by Kevin Horton; Full Game by Doug Fraker (MIT); Thwaite by Damian Yerrick (GPL-3.0, source at pinobatch/thwaite-nes ). License nesformer is released under the MIT License (see LICENSE ). The ROMs in roms/ keep their own licenses, listed in roms/SOURCES.md . title: Azure's Weakest Link – Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises
body_text: Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Azureâs Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises | Binary Security AS Home About Careers Services Penetration Testing Application Security Security Engineering Posts Contact Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises Posted by Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud on October 02, 2026 · 18 mins read In my previous blog posts, Azureâs Weakest Link? and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , I gave an overview of the severely insecure architecture behind API Connections in Azure, a part of Azure Logic Apps, and an instance of a full cross-tenant compromise using these inherent flaws. Now I am back with some more vulnerabilities in this system, each giving the same primitives to the attacker. In total, the vulnerabilities here netted me a cool $200,000. I also held a talk detailing this at Blue Hat Asia 2026, and when the recordings are out, I will add a link here. TL;DR API Connections allow anyone to fully compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend. This includes cross-tenant compromise of Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, as well as any other externally connected service, such as Jira or Salesforce. The only thing stopping exploitation is really the layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, but as you will see, it is really difficult to catch all the edge cases here. Architecture If you havenât read the first parts of this series, I would recommend checking those out first, Azureâs Weakest Link? - Part 1 and Azureâs Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise , but if you donât care, I will go through the most important parts of the architecture first. From Microsoftâs documentation , we see a quite intriguing diagram of how the API Connection architecture is built. This basically spells out all that is needed to understand how the system operates, kudos to whoever made it! It works like this A logic app, the symbol on the bottom left, queries a shared Azure API Management instance The API Management instance first checks the swagger (OpenAPI) definition of the connector type and checks that it is a valid action A sort of key exchange happens where the input token, or key, is exchanged for the configured token for the backend service The API Management instance finishes the call with this new token to the backend instance. From this, we can surmise that if we are able to trick the API Management instance to operate on a different connection than the ones we own, we would be able to effectively use the configured token for a victimâs connection on their backend service. This service can, in effect, be anything. As you can see here , the list of backend services is effectively unbounded and includes a number of Azure services. However great the diagram is, there is one crucial omission, which we have already used to great effect in part 2 of this series. By using the ARM REST API DynamicInvoke or /extensions/proxy/ endpoints, we can directly query the APIM service through ARM. I have taken the liberty of updating the diagram to match this. Considering this, and the fact that, as a resource manager, ARM basically has full access to everything, our exploitation pathway becomes clear. We must trick the calling service into querying a different connection than ours, and thus get full control of the backend service. Caveat: It is, of course, possible for the people who set up these connections to scope their access tokens or keys so that the API Connection has minimal privileges in the backend. I would guess, however, that this is rarely done. In the case of OAuth connections, it will surely always be the token of the person who initially made the connection. And for the API key case, well, who cares enough to scope such things minimally? Microsoft doesnât, at least. Initial Exploitation The first cross-tenant exploitation I achieved in API Connections, and in fact in Azure as a whole, has already been described in part 2. As a recap, here is an example payload using the DynamicInvoke endpoint of my own connection to read the Key Vault of a different tenant. POST /subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom2/DynamicInvoke?api-version=2018-07-01-preview HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Type : application/json Content-Length : 147 { "request" :{ "method" : "get" , "path" : "path/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value" }, } HTTP/2 200 OK Cache-Control: no-cache Pragma: no-cache Content-Length: 1329 { "response": { "statusCode": "OK", "body": { "value": "dontreadme", "name": "victimsecret", "version": "7914d45aa60342809fb8cc12dc68b10e", "contentType": null, "isEnabled": true, "createdTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "lastUpdatedTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z", "validityStartTime": null, "validityEndTime": null }, "headers": { <Headers> } } } As you can see, itâs a pretty clear path traversal vulnerability. This implies what we already assumed: When the request fires from ARM to the APIM instance, it has rights to all connections, regardless of what it operates on. Further exploitation A couple of weeks after I reported this vulnerability, it got marked as fixed, and when I tried it again, the following error message greeted me: Now, I considered whether or not this was a sufficient fix. It seemed to restrict the paths allowed, rather than the underlying token issue, so I guessed there would be ways around it. An interesting little fact about the ARM API is that, in some cases, it might not be as much of a black box as you assume. The relevant code can sometimes be found within the resource types themselves. I do not know whether this code actually executes on these machines or is merely included as an artifact, but it is a gold mine of interesting information. So, I created a Standard Logic App, which provides a fully dedicated host, SSHed into it, and extracted the code. Lo and behold, look what I found: Can you see the fix they implemented? What was even more interesting here actually was something I found, and was not really even looking for. When searching for the actual DynamicInvoke code, what greeted me was not actually just this one public function, but four: These functions are completely undocumented, and I could find no reference to them anywhere. However, they were reachable and located along the same path. So, for instance, to hit DynamicList here, simply change dynamicInvoke in your URI to DynamicList . Knowing that the slap-dash blacklisting fix that they implemented only applied to DynamicInvoke , I assumed that these would all be vulnerable in the same way if they had the same functionality. Without boring you too much with the required arguments and return values here, the exploitation method is really quite the same, although the payload is a bit more involved. For DynamicList , you need to specify each path parameter on its own and do a bit of work to get a result, but the same logic applies. To achieve, for instance, a cross-tenant write on a victimâs SQL server through their connection, a payload like this works: POST /subscriptions/162fc6db-03cd-4fe8-ab44-dc0a947e74af/resourceGroups/api-connection/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom_validator/DynamicList?api-version=2018-07-01-preview&_=1765372176638 HTTP / 2 Host : management.azure.com Authorization : Bearer <token> Content-Length : 524 Content-Type : application/json { "dynamicInvocationDefinition" : { "operationID" : "nine" , "parameters" : { "one" : { "value" : ".." }, "two" : { "value" : ".." }, "three" : { "value" : "sql" }, "four" : { "value" : "88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c" }, "five" : { "value" : "v2" }, "six" : { "value" : "datasets" }, "seven" : { "value" : "victimservice.database.windows.net,VictimDatabase" }, "eigth" : { "value" : "query" }, "nine" : { "value" : "sql" }, "query" : { "value" : { "query" : "Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3)" } } }, "ItemsPath" : "ResultSets/Table1" , "ItemValuePath" : "secrets" , "ItemTitlePath" : "value" } } You can quite easily see that the first parameters here execute the path traversal and then perform an arbitrary SQL query on the database. I reported only the DynamicList case first, in the hope that they would perform a similar fix to DynamicInvoke and I would get to report on the other two as well. Sadly, their fix involved simply blocking all these endpoints. No other mitigations seem to be in place, however, so if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable. Further exploitation Messing around with paths in these dynamic calls seemed to have reached its conclusion: I couldnât get past the path limitations on DynamicInvoke , and all the other endpoints were blocked. What I needed was a different way in. As I was trying to sleep one day, it occurred to me that I had overlooked using the Logic Apps themselves. I realized that there was, in fact, a significant difference between the Consumption and Standard Logic Apps connection-creation flows. The most glaring difference is that Consumption Logic Apps, where your workflow is co-located with a bunch of others, create a Version 1 connection, while the dedicated-host Standard Logic Apps create a Version 2 connection. The following diagrams make a more subtle difference between the flows clear: Do you see the difference? Obviously, when itâs spelled out like that, itâs pretty clear what the point is. Using a Standard Logic App, after we have created the resource and added whatever authentication to the backend server we need, we authorize that specific logic app to access it using its managed identity. However, when we have a Consumption Logic App, we donât have any such identity to authorize because we donât control it. This perhaps makes some sense: we canât authorize it, so we donât. I realized that this must imply that every Consumption Logic App has implicit access to every Version 1 API Connection; the only thing stopping us from exploiting this must be some sort of input validation. The classic view of a Logic App workflow is quite restrictive in its input, but there are both the API endpoints, and the Code view in the GUI that allow us to play around a bit more with the inputs. This allows us to see the inputs in more detail, edit them, and even add more. The obvious trick of changing the referenced connector to a victimâs connection fails, as the runtime performs extensive validation that you own the connection. We have the codebase, though, so we can try to find all the valid parameters. It did not take much searching for me to discover the host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter. I canât quite get my head around why this parameter is included, nor why itâs still accepted to this day, but it works in the way you would expect. After performing a series of validations on the connection referenced in host.connection , you can specify that it should use something completely different instead of the runtimeUrl baked into that connection. As long as the host ends with azure-apihub.net , it will also include the required Authorization header. What happens when this workflow is run then? The keen-eyed reader might notice that the runtimeUrl used in the exploit is not just the connectionId . This is because some extra elements get added to the URI, but it is of no consequence to us; the exploit works fine. Manna from the heavens I, of course, reported this to Microsoft again, and they spent some time working up a fix. When it finally came through, the exploit returned an error message: The host API runtime URL is not valid for the API connection '/subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/keyvault-1'. The runtime URL path must match the expected API endpoint 'https://logic-apis-norwayeast.azure-apihub.net/apim/keyvault/cbfb0f4313144117a7440368902bb871?' for the referenced connection. Either omit the 'host.api' input property, or correct the runtime URL to match the API associated with the connection. Except for the excessive length of this message, it seems like quite a suitable fix. The runtime URL must exactly match what is expected; otherwise, no dice. Apart from just removing the parameter altogether, itâs quite sane. Unless, of course, it checks that value at the wrong time: This works again, with the same result. Whatâs going on here is that the validation happens before the path is normalized, so the runtime thinks the URI is pointing to my referenced connection, but the APIM instance sees it differently. And just like that, I got another critical vulnerability. The fun does not stop there. When Microsoft managed to scrape together a fix for this path traversal, a surprising thing happened. The original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated, and as a result, you could perform that attack again. I would include some pictures, but they would be the same pictures as above, so you can just imagine them. Reporting and rewards Altogether, API Connections have netted me five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in Azure, which is perhaps more than expected. All vulnerabilities reported here were fixed within a reasonable time after I submitted the reports, and while there were some disagreements with MSRC along the way, overall, I am quite happy with the results. What's next Special Thanks ../ Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? Wed Oct 28 2026 authored by veritas Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js . A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg } Huh? function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation. I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts. Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research. Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request. I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked. Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!
