title: The federated code forge
body_text: The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog The federated code forge Anirudh 30 October 2026 For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation. But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however. ’05 Mail + Git ’09 GitHub + Git ’25 AT Protocol + Git Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge. It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose , you can still talk to everyone else. Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack . Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge. Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly . The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become y o u r c o d e f o r g e f o r t h e n e x t d e c a d e . Product updates A fresh look! The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans . A bobbin near you Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden. This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin . Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance. The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services. The new data model and repo-owned data First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.* , replacing the old sh.tangled.* records. Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary. With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way. In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose. But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability. If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification! Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide . Organizations Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs . Stacked PRs for everyone Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well. Launch weeks ahead This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent. Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally. Your code, your network. Come build with us on Tangled. Sign up © 2026 Tangled Labs Oy. Tangled Docs Source Discord Bluesky X/Twitter Terms Privacy

title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
body_text: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dhruv Mehrotra Maddy Varner Dell Cameron Security Oct 28, 2026 4:00 PM Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents The leaked records include the locations of ICE and CBP facilities, workers’ cell phone numbers, and the members of groups tied to wiretap programs, Palantir software, and xAI’s Grok chatbot. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents , including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119 , a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool. “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.” Updated 10/28/2026 at 8:02 pm ET: Added comment from DHS. Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: Go inside the world of digital security with Kernel Panic We sexted with a Muse AI agent —and Meta says that’s totally fine Big Story: Meet the DEA’s premier crypto detective OpenAI is pissing off mathematicians Want better search results? Make WIRED a preferred source in Google Written by WIRED Staff Topics immigration Department of Homeland Security Immigration and Customs Enforcement Customs and Border Protection privacy cybersecurity First Amendment free speech hackers hacking Read More ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations is engaged in far-reaching spying against left-wing activists that rivals the FBI and CIA crackdowns on the Civil Rights and anti-war movements. Ali Winston Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records Bluesky tells WIRED it blocked links to a leaked archive of information on 41,000 ICE, CBP, and other DHS workers because it contains people’s contact information, shared without their authorization. Dhruv Mehrotra ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity in Maine, but stored information about them in a database run on Palantir software, newly unsealed court filings say. Maddy Varner ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud Documents obtained by Democracy Forward show that ICE looked into feeding voter roll data into the ELITE tool, normally used to identify targets for deportation. David Gilbert Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists Despite Illinois’ sanctuary laws, local police in and around Chicago helped ICE investigative agents track activists engaged in First Amendment–protected activities. Ali Winston The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans Two US senators say the Trump administration is breaking the law by withholding the FISA court decision while it presses Congress to renew America’s most sweeping surveillance program. Dell Cameron A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System Sources tell WIRED that an Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Vittoria Elliott Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy As a recent government report on DOGE shows, even getting basic information out of the Trump administration will put a new Congress to the test. Vittoria Elliott Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls From heat maps to Signal chats to war rooms, volunteers across the US are ready to act if federal immigration agents show up on Election Day. David Gilbert ICE Agent at NYC Shooting Has History of Alleged Violence and Illegal Arrests Brenden Cuni, an ICE supervisor, has been accused of excessive force and tackling a pregnant woman to the ground. Several of his arrests were later found to be unlawful in federal court. Dhruv Mehrotra Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer Investigators also sought permission to use an invasive surveillance tool called a cell-site simulators against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate. Dhruv Mehrotra A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There Despite the agency's human resources department saying he hadn’t even been onboarded, Jeremy Lewin oversaw the destruction of USAID. It’s not clear he had the legal authority to do so. Molly Knight Raskin WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. Through rigorous investigations and game-changing reporting, we tell stories that don’t just reflect the moment—they help create it. When you look back in 10, 20, even 50 years, WIRED will be the publication that led the story of the present, mapped the people, products, and ideas defining it, and explained how those forces forged the future. We won't "just hang out"
body_text: We Won’t “Just Hang Out” Home ❖ Blog We Won’t “Just Hang Out” 28 October, 2026 Detail from Wall Street , Paul Strand , 1915. What will we do after the Singularity? The standard answer is: “we’ll just hang out”. The infinite vacation, as in the Culture novels. I think this won’t work. “Hanging out” implies: Other people exist. They want to hang out with you. You want to hang out with them. And the post-scarcity, infinite vacation AI utopia undermines all these assumptions. Other people exist The social processes by which people come together and build relationships will disappear. Work, obviously, is pointless in a world of cheap superhuman intelligence. University (really all education beyond teaching people to speak) will be pointless because there’s no work to do and because growing your human capital doesn’t change your life outcomes: you get the same UBI whether you’re illiterate or a PhD. I met a lot of my friends by writing open-source code, and participating in the community of software engineers. AI is dissolving that community by making human contributions superfluous . If Claude Code has existed when I was starting out, nobody would have cared about Austral or my other open-source projects or my technical blog posts. As a teenager I tried to install Linux, ran into all kinds of problems, and went on the IRC chatrooms to get help. And in the process I made friends. Today, I would just ask Claude. AI disintermediates everyone, so that we no longer need each other. I still have friends, but I’m running off this pre-AI supply of friends I met through communities of practice. Young people don’t have that privilege. What even is the point of cities in a world without work? If there’s nothing to do, there is no need to bring people together geographically. They want to hang out with you The BATNA to hanging out keeps getting better, cheaper, and more convenient. When people’s sensorium becomes an infinite firehose of AI-generated superstimulus, why would they hang out with anyone? This is less about AI and more about the trajectory of consumer technology, since many people already live like this: they go to work and watch TikTok. After work, they will just watch TikTok. You want to hang out with them As Gregory Conti explains : [Under] ASI this endless leisure will be passed in diminished, tiresome company, since we will lack the experiences of struggle and striving that generate interesting personalities. Our minds will have atrophied. We will have little of note to say to one another. The people in the AI utopia will have no skills, no education, no accomplishments. We’ll be lucky if they are even literate. They will not be worth talking to, and you won’t want to hang out with them. Maybe you and I can hang out with our existing friends. But just iterate this a bit. What about the next generation? How are they going to build meaningful relationships where the social processes that built those relationships are all in the past? If we get radical life extension, there’s the problem of attrition over the long term: people will drift apart, drop out of society to enter the experience machine, die in accidents, or end their lives out of ennui. So your social network might be a non-renewable resource that gets exhausted over time as your pre-Singularity relationships attrite and can’t be replaced for the reasons above. title: Patrick Stewart has died
Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS
body_text: SMS of Death: zero-click Android telephony DoS SMS OF DEATH Vulnerability Impact Why it matters PoC Android Telephony Â· Zero-Click Â· Remote DoS SMS of Death A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls ( including emergency calls ), with zero interaction from the victim. Download APK Source â Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading. Component WapPushOverSms frameworks/opt/telephony Interaction None zero-click, silent Vector Remote SMS WAP Push, port 2948 Affected Android 12â17 patched in 14â17, Oct 2026 update Reporter Mark B Reported 5 May 2026 Android & Devices VRP Disclosed 29 Oct 2026 public writeup Recovery ADB only normal user: bricked 01 / The vulnerability An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar . The value comes back as a long , is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array: // WapPushOverSms.java:217 header length read as long, cast with no bounds check int headerLength = ( int ) pduDecoder.getValue32(); ... // WapPushOverSms.java:244 the cast value is used as an array size byte [] header = new byte [headerLength]; A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000 . Cast to a signed 32-bit int , that is -2147483648 . Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone : E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648 E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244) E AndroidRuntime: at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169) E AndroidRuntime: at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627) The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number. Affected versions. The code sits in Android's core telephony framework and has shipped in many releases. The crash has been reproduced from Android 12 (the reboot loop in issue #2 ) up to Android 16 . Google's October 2026 fix was released for Android 14 through 17 , so devices on older versions outside the security-update window, such as Android 12 and 13, run the same code and do not receive the fix. 02 / Impact Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort Zero-click. The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification. Silent. Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown. Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts. Telephony blackout. 1-2 seconds of no service per message while com.android.phone restarts. Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing. ~20 messages render the device unusable for an extended period. Persistent denial of service. The malformed message stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below). Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate. Recovery over ADB, contributed by @sakisdog After hitting the reboot loop on Android 12 , @sakisdog documented a less destructive recovery ( issue #2 ). The poison messages sit in the pending inbound queue ( content://sms/raw ) and are retried on every boot, so Android's RescueParty reboots the device into recovery roughly every 90 seconds. Deleting just those rows over ADB, in the short window after boot completes, breaks the loop with no factory reset: # while sys.boot_completed == 1: find the WAP Push rows (destination_port=134020), note the address adb shell content query --uri content://sms/raw --projection _id:destination_port:date:deleted # let the shell edit SMS storage, delete only those rows, then reset the permission adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS allow adb shell "content delete --uri content://sms/raw --where \"address='<SENDER>'\"" adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS default # last resort, erases ALL SMS/MMS and APN settings: adb shell pm clear com.android.providers.telephony Recovery credited to @sakisdog . It still needs a computer and ADB, and you should not choose "wipe data" at the recovery prompt, so for a non-technical user mid-loop it remains out of reach. This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service that, left untreated, reboots the phone into a recovery wipe-data prompt every ~90 seconds, driving a normal user to a factory reset to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's published rules. 03 / Why this is serious A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or stuck in the reboot loop, it cannot reliably place a call to 000 . The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing. Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination , administered by the ACMA , carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset . Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days. The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network , not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until it is updated. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand. The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces. Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination Â· Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination Â· Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis 04 / The fix One bounds check The remedy is a range check before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (line 217) , provided to Google on the day of the first report: long rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32(); if (rawHeaderLen < 0 || rawHeaderLen > pdu.length) { result.statusCode = Intents.RESULT_SMS_GENERIC_ERROR; return result; } int headerLength = ( int ) rawHeaderLen; What Google shipped Google fixed this crash, but not with the bounds check above. On 15 June 2026 an Android engineer authored commit 735d967 , "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," which shipped in the October 2026 Android security release for Android 14 through 17. Rather than validate the length, it widens the caught exception so the crash is swallowed, and deletes the triggering message so it cannot re-crash on carrier redelivery or on boot: // WapPushOverSms.java: widen the catch to cover NegativeArraySizeException - } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aie) { + } catch (RuntimeException e) { // InboundSmsHandler.java: a failed decode now deletes the poison message + try { success = processMessagePart(tracker); } + catch (RuntimeException e) { deleteFromRawTable(...); } // breaks the boot loop This fix is part of the October 2026 Android security update. Devices updated to the October 2026 patch level or later are protected; devices on earlier patch levels remain vulnerable. 05 / Proof of concept Source & APK The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number. Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing. Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries. The software is provided "as is", with no warranty, under the Apache License 2.0 . The author accepts no liability for any use, misuse, or damage. By downloading the APK or the source, you accept full responsibility for what you do with it. Download APK Source on GitHub Full disclosure by Mark B Â· @sourone github.com/MarkBlah/smsofdeath Â· Apache 2.0 Â· 2026

title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
body_text: Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5 - Divyansh Agrawal d ↗ My writing Series Attention Lab Chipformer My work About Résumé ↗ Contact ↗ ← My writing COMPILED WEIGHTS Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5 A stock Qwen 3.5 4B with a RISC-V CPU compiled into its weights, running on its own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM. Series Qwenputer Part 1 of 3 ↗ By Divyansh Agrawal 22 October 2026 9 min read Markdown version 👏 ... Save Email address Subscribe On this page I can't believe it's not silicon The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Compiling a computer into layers The CPU How Qwen uses it Does it work? A hard drive? In this economy? Limits and what's next Beyond arithmetic Try it Get new articles by email I can't believe it's not silicon Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide .) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever. To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage. I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with . Qwen hands a multiplication to the RISC-V CPU inside its own weights; the CPU's RAM is Gated DeltaNet state You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope , and the code is on GitHub . The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism ( more on that here ). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated. Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1, 1 1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1, 2 2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding, 3 3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache. Gated DeltaNet state used as RAM: a one-hot key overwrites one row, a one-hot query reads it back, and the CPU keeps its registers, memory and program counter in those rows The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights". 4 4 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it. This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment. Compiling a computer into layers Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes. Each instruction becomes a few generated tokens: one names the memory row to write (ADDR), the next carries the value (VAL), and a STEP token ends the instruction. Those tokens are the CPU's execution trace, so while Qwen is generating them, the CPU is actually running. The CPU The CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus the Zba extension and a small bignum unit for big-number arithmetic), and it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32. As it stands, it passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error. 5 5 Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps. This CPU can also run C and MicroPython code in the forward passes quite well (although a bit slowly). It is not a Linux-class chip yet, but it implements the full RV32IM instruction set. How Qwen uses it Qwen 3.5 4B is able to use this CPU quite well, without any post-training required. The CPU is used completely internally, and not invoked through any external tool calls. In order to make the model use this reliably, I decided to go the cheap way: by piggybacking on the tool call format that models are quite well-trained on, Qwen sends the CPU its instructions and reads back the results. No external tool calls or runtime are used. Once our CPU receives the instructions, the computer layers run, and then write the tool response. We use a small driver called RvChat to load the firmware into the GDN state, and this keeps the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers. Qwen's original weights stay exactly as they are. The computer weights are added on top of them, in extra dims and layers. Does it work? I think the main question here on your mind after reading through my incessant ranting will be: does this actually work? Accuracy of base Qwen3.5-4B, Qwenputer and base Qwen with a Python tool on NUPA and DeepMind arithmetic sets On the DeepMind sets: div_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 95% by giving Qwen 3.5 4B a Python tool and 72.5% for base Qwen. mul_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 100% with a Python tool and 55% for base Qwen. mul_div_multiple_longer: Qwenputer scores 100%, versus 97.5% with a Python tool and 90% for base Qwen. add_or_sub_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, the same as with a Python tool, and 87.5% for base Qwen. On NUPA's long-integer arithmetic, Qwenputer goes from 48.6% to 100%, the same as giving Qwen a Python tool. The numbers the CPU prints are exact, too: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions against a reference machine and found zero mismatches. And bolting a computer onto Qwen doesn't change how it talks: its normal text stays within noise of base Qwen (KL 6e-4, against a noise floor of 5e-4). A hard drive? In this economy? Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too. Since we already have a functional RAM, this was mostly trivial. On the model side, it's exposed via internal put / append / get / list / delete operations. Once again, no actual tool calls. When Qwen 'saves' a file, the compiled layers hash its name into one of 1,024 slots in a directory kept in the DeltaNet state, and store the text itself in other heads, with eight tokens per row, chained together. In scenarios where two names end up landing on the same slot, it just checks the next one. Finding a file again takes roughly two or three steps instead of a scan, and it holds up to 512 files, which comes out to about 53,000 tokens of text. Fun thing is, this is quite persistent. You can save the state at the end of a conversation, load it into the next one, and the files are still there. Using this filesystem, Qwen gets facts that changed between chats right 90% of the time, against 30% when you paste the old chats back in, and it's on par with giving Qwen memory tools run by Python (83.3% vs 78.9%). This one is still experimental, and its code lives on the rv-store branch , with the model on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Limits and what's next Qwenputer is very much an experiment, so a few limitations. The extra layers and wider hidden size make the checkpoint 18.8 GB, roughly double base Qwen, although most of it is zero padding. It also needs a small driver (RvChat) to boot the firmware and keep the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers, so it doesn't run with a plain generate() call yet. And it's a bit slow, with every CPU instruction costing a few decoded tokens, so a big calculation takes seconds rather than milliseconds. The batched executor I used for the benchmarks runs about 3,200 CPU tokens a second on an L4. Next up, I want Qwen to write Python and run it on the MicroPython inside its own weights, through a python() tool that works the same way calc does. Making the CPU faster is the other big one. Beyond arithmetic Exact control over the RNN layers is useful for a lot more than arithmetic. It also makes Qwenputer a really nice testbed for AI safety research, and I wrote up two follow-ups: how hybrid models like Qwen 3.5 can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights can work as monitorability tools , like an in-weight monitor the model can't switch off, or answer keys for interpretability. Try it If you want to play with it yourself, the model runs on a single 24 GB GPU. You'll need uv and the Hugging Face CLI. You don't need a tool server or a Python sandbox for the calculations: the CPU runs them inside the model. git clone https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer && cd qwenputer/experimental/riscv && uv sync --extra hf hf download divagr1925/Qwen3.5-4B-Qwenputer --local-dir qwenputer-rv uv run python -m chipformer.rv.chat qwenputer-rv --firmware tests/data/rv/calc-bridge.elf \ --ask "Use calc: what is 123456789 * 987654321?" Everything is open: the code on GitHub , and both models on Hugging Face ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ) and ModelScope ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ). If you use it in your work, you can cite it as: @software{agrawal2026qwenputer, author = {Agrawal, Divyansh}, title = {{Qwenputer}: a computer compiled into the weights of a pretrained language model}, year = {2026}, url = {https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer} } Notes Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. ↩ After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. ↩ A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. ↩ Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. ↩ Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps. ↩ Get new articles by email Email address Subscribe ← My writing Newer article Hybrid models can hide reasoning in their RNN state Older article Consensus Is Not Corroboration RELATED POSTS Building oversight tools into a model's weights ↗ Hybrid models can hide reasoning in their RNN state ↗ GET IN TOUCH [email protected] ↗ © 2026 DIVYANSH AGRAWAL GITHUB · X · LINKEDIN BACK TO TOP ↑

title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
body_text: H.264 is magic: a technical walkthrough of a remarkable technology. Sid Bala Home LinkedIn GitHub Sign in Subscribe H.264 is Magic Sid Bala 02 Nov 2016 • 10 min read Share H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now. H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video. Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264. Why even compress anything? A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue). 1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ 370 MB/sec of raw data. This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1]. So yeah. We need compression. Why H.264 compression? Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage: I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files: PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB 5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched. No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB. It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG. How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick? There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones. Shedding weight Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that. You remove everything except the things that matter. This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits. PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image. Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important? There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this. What does H.264 actually do? H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard. See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs! 7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that? For this we need a quick math lesson. Information Entropy Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset. For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense? Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy . The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data. Frequency Domain Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok! Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough. Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY? freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain: The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense? In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image. Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this? Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be. Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied. The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs! So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization [^3]. Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got? Chroma Subsampling. The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight. In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy. Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you? Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally. But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs! This process of discarding some of the color information is called Chroma Subsampling [^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally. Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information. Wait. That's it? Can we do something more? Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time. Motion compensation H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard. Motion compensation? What now? Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right? Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation? Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an I-frame (Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either P-frames (predicted) or B-frames (bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame. B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around. Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause? Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that? Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you. Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation. Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video. Looks pretty good to me. Now what? Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure. Entropy Coder The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video. An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in. And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks. Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now. The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get: 5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => 1.2 GB Compressed video => 175 KB If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get 0.4 lbs as the final weight. 6.5 ounces! Yeah. It's magic! Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive. Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use HackerNews or Reddit for voicing your opinion! Or hit me up on Twitter or LinkedIn if you want to chat. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window. Install Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin . Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app . For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications. Windows Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1 | iex Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. Find your work A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as: Working: still busy. Blocked: waiting for you. Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere. Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine. The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. Work on another machine Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. Make it yours Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format. Layouts and mods · Commands Updates and privacy Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves. Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod. For agents herdr-app --skill This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. herdr-app ls herdr-app status herdr-app commands The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments. Build from source For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing . Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI . Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git cd herdr-app just build just test just install Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages. To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: python scripts/bench.py --bin < app executable > --set spinners --seconds 20 The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py . Breadcrumb Home Innovation & AI Models & research Gemini Models Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.
